rungs.why: (⇐) Assume $u$ is an upper bound satisfying the $\varepsilon$-condition. Take any $v<u$ and turn the gap into an $\varepsilon$.
Apply the hypothesis with this specific $\varepsilon$ to get a point of $S$ beating $v$.
rungs.m: $$\exists\, s_\varepsilon\in S:\ u-\varepsilon < s_\varepsilon \iff v < s_\varepsilon$$

rungs.why: So no $v<u$ can be an upper bound of $S$ — exactly condition (2) of the supremum definition.
rungs.m: $$v<u \Rightarrow v \text{ is not an upper bound} \Rightarrow u=\sup S$$

rungs.why: (⇒) Conversely, suppose $u=\sup S$ and let $\varepsilon>0$ be given. Since $u$ is the LEAST upper bound, anything strictly below it fails to be one.
rungs.m: $$u-\varepsilon < u \Rightarrow u-\varepsilon \text{ is not an upper bound of } S$$

rungs.why: "Not an upper bound" means, by definition, some element of $S$ slips past it.
Start from a nonempty $S$ bounded below by $w$; build the sign-flipped set.
"$w$ is a lower bound of $S$" becomes, after flipping signs, "$-w$ is an upper bound of $S'$".
rungs.m: $$s\ge w\ \forall s\in S \iff -s\le -w\ \forall s\in S \ \Rightarrow\ S' \text{ bounded above by } -w$$

rungs.why: Now apply the Completeness Property (the axiom) to the bounded-above set $S'$.
Claim $-u = \inf S$; check both defining conditions by flipping signs back.
rungs.m: $$-u \le s\ \forall s\in S \quad(\text{lower bound}),\qquad t\le s\ \forall s\in S \Rightarrow t\le -u \quad(\text{greatest such})$$

rungs.why: Suppose, for contradiction, both $x'$ and $x''$ are limits of $(x_n)$.
Split an arbitrary tolerance in half — one half for each limit — so the two errors will add up to exactly $\varepsilon$ at the end.
rungs.m: $$\text{given }\varepsilon>0,\ \exists K': n\ge K' \Rightarrow |x_n-x'|<\varepsilon/2$$ $$\exists K'': n\ge K'' \Rightarrow |x_n-x''|<\varepsilon/2$$

rungs.why: Take $n$ large enough to satisfy both conditions simultaneously.
Insert and subtract $x_n$ (add-and-subtract trick), then apply the triangle inequality.
Proof of (a): Given $\varepsilon > 0$, apply the Archimedean Property (2.4.3) to find $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with $K > 1/\varepsilon$.
Proof of (c): Since $0 < b < 1$, write $b = \frac{1}{1 + a}$ where $a = \frac{1}{b} - 1 > 0$. Apply Bernoulli's Inequality (2.1.13).
Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with $K > \frac{1}{a \varepsilon}$.
Proof of (e): Let $x_n := n^{1/n} - 1$. Since $n \ge 1$, $x_n \ge 0$. Expand $n = (1 + x_n)^n$ via the Binomial Theorem for $n \ge 2$.
Isolate $x_n^2$: subtract 1 and divide by $\frac{n(n - 1)}{2} > 0$.
Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $K > 2/\varepsilon^2$. Then $n \ge K \implies |n^{1/n} - 1| = x_n \le \sqrt{2/n} < \varepsilon$.

title: Subsequences of convergent sequences converge to the same limit

rungs.why: Start from what convergence of $X$ already gives us.
Key fact about any strictly increasing sequence of indices: by induction, the $k$-th chosen index is never smaller than $k$ itself.
So once $k$ reaches $K(\varepsilon)$, the corresponding original index $n_k$ has already reached $K(\varepsilon)$ too, and the original bound applies.
(i) If $X$ converged to some $x$, then by c.3.4.2 every subsequence — including $X'$ and $X''$ — would have to converge to that same $x$.
rungs.m: $$X\to x \ \Rightarrow\ X'\to x \text{ and } X''\to x$$

rungs.why: But we are given two subsequences with DIFFERENT limits — contradiction, so $X$ cannot converge.
rungs.m: $$\lim X' \ne \lim X'' \ \Rightarrow\ \text{no such } x \text{ can exist}$$

rungs.why: (ii) A convergent sequence eventually sits inside a fixed neighbourhood of its limit; the finitely many terms before that are automatically bounded (any finite set of numbers is bounded).
So convergent $\Rightarrow$ bounded; taking the contrapositive gives unbounded $\Rightarrow$ divergent.
Define what makes a term unbeatable from that point onward.
rungs.m: $$x_m \text{ is a peak if } x_m \ge x_n \text{ for all } n\ge m$$

rungs.why: Case 1 — infinitely many peaks exist. List them in increasing order of index; being a peak means each one is $\ge$ every later term, in particular the next peak.
Case 2 — only finitely many peaks exist. Start just past the last peak, where nothing is a peak any longer.
"Not a peak" means, by definition, some strictly later term beats it. Chase that bigger term, then repeat the chase from there, forever.
rungs.m: $$x_{s_1}\text{ not a peak} \Rightarrow \exists\, s_2>s_1: x_{s_2}>x_{s_1} \Rightarrow \exists\, s_3>s_2: x_{s_3}>x_{s_2} \Rightarrow \cdots$$

rungs.why: Start from what we already proved about the ORDER of any sequence — it always hides a monotone thread inside it.
rungs.m: $$X=(x_n) \text{ bounded} \ \Rightarrow\ X \text{ has a monotone subsequence } X'=(x_{n_k}) \quad\text{(by Monotone Subsequence Thm, §3.4)}$$

rungs.why: A subsequence of a bounded sequence is still bounded — you have only removed terms, never added any wilder new ones.

Now $X'$ is BOTH monotone and bounded — exactly the hypothesis of the Monotone Convergence Theorem, whose proof is where completeness actually gets used: a bounded increasing sequence converges to its supremum.
rungs.m: $$X' \text{ monotone} + \text{bounded} \ \Rightarrow\ X' \text{ converges} \quad\text{(Monotone Convergence Thm, §3.3, via Completeness, §2.3)}$$

rungs.why: That convergent $X'$ IS a subsequence of the original $X$ — exactly what we set out to find.
rungs.m: $$\therefore\ X \text{ has a convergent subsequence } X'$$

title: Convergence Criterion via limsup and liminf

rungs.why: Notice that for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$, $x_m \in \{x_n : n \ge m\}$, which directly gives the fundamental sandwich inequality.
rungs.m: $$u_m = \inf\{x_n : n \ge m\} \le x_m \le \sup\{x_n : n \ge m\} = v_m \quad \text{for all } m \in \mathbb{N}$$

rungs.why: (⇐) Suppose $\limsup(x_n) = \liminf(x_n) = L$. By definition of limit superior and inferior, $\lim(u_m) = L$ and $\lim(v_m) = L$.
Apply the Squeeze Theorem (3.2.4) to the inequality $u_m \le x_m \le v_m$.
(⇒) Conversely, suppose $\lim(x_n) = x$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $K \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x - \varepsilon < x_n < x + \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge K$.
Then for any $m \ge K$, $x + \varepsilon$ is an upper bound and $x - \varepsilon$ is a lower bound for the tail $\{x_n : n \ge m\}$.
rungs.m: $$x - \varepsilon \le u_m \le v_m \le x + \varepsilon \quad \text{for all } m \ge K$$

rungs.why: Take the limit as $m \to \infty$ to conclude that both $\liminf$ and $\limsup$ lie in $[x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon]$.
Since $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary, this forces equality.
(⇒) Assume $\lim_{x\to c}f=L$; take ANY sequence $(x_n)$ in $A\setminus\{c\}$ with $(x_n)\to c$. We must show $(f(x_n))\to L$. Start from the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ promise.
Now use $(x_n)\to c$: feed THIS $\delta$ into the sequence's own convergence to $c$ to get an index $K$ that traps $x_n$ within $\delta$ of $c$.
Combine: past $K$, $x_n$ is within $\delta$ of $c$ (and $\ne c$ by hypothesis), so the $\delta$-promise from step 1 fires and controls $f(x_n)$.

(⇐) Prove the CONTRAPOSITIVE instead: assume $f$ does NOT have limit $L$ at $c$, and construct one specific bad sequence. Negating "$\forall\varepsilon\,\exists\delta\ldots$" means one bad $\varepsilon_0$ defeats every $\delta$.
Apply this with $\delta=1/n$ for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ — one bad point per shrinking neighbourhood — to manufacture a whole sequence.
Check this sequence really does converge to $c$ (the $1/n$ bound forces it, by squeeze), while its image sequence provably never gets close to $L$.
State the Sequential Criterion (c.4.1.8): $\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$ iff for all sequences $(x_n)$ in $A \setminus \{c\}$ with $x_n \to c$, $f(x_n) \to L$.
rungs.m: What this really means: For a function limit to exist, every possible sequence of stepping stones approaching $c$ must force the function values to approach the exact same target $L$.

rungs.why: Negate the equivalence for part (a): $\lim_{x\to c} f(x) \ne L$ if and only if there is at least one sequence $(x_n)$ with $x_n \to c$ but $f(x_n) \not\to L$.
rungs.m: What this really means: To disprove that $L$ is the limit, you don't have to test infinitely many sequences—you only need to find a single rogue path heading to $c$ whose values miss $L$.

rungs.why: For part (b), $f$ has no limit in $\mathbb{R}$ at all if and only if no candidate $L$ works; either some $(f(x_n))$ diverges entirely, or two sequences produce distinct limits.
rungs.m: What this really means: To prove a function has no limit whatsoever, produce two separate sequences heading to $c$ that end up at two completely different destinations, or one sequence that shoots off to infinity or oscillates wildy.

rungs.why: Negate the claim: suppose some real number $x$ IS an upper bound for the whole set $\mathbb{N}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: To see why counting can never be trapped, we imagine the opposite: suppose there exists a giant brick wall $x$ on the number line that no counting number $1, 2, 3, \ldots$ can ever climb over.

rungs.why: Then $\mathbb{N}$ is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ bounded above, so the Completeness Property applies.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If natural numbers really were blocked by a ceiling, the completeness of the real numbers guarantees there must be an exact, tightest possible ceiling $u$ right above them.

rungs.why: $u-1$ is strictly smaller than the LEAST upper bound $u$, so it cannot itself be an upper bound of $\mathbb{N}$.
rungs.m: $$u-1<u \ \Rightarrow\ u-1 \text{ is not an upper bound of } \mathbb{N}$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If you step just one full stride backwards from this tightest ceiling to $u-1$, you drop below the ceiling, landing right back inside the territory where counting numbers live.

rungs.why: "Not an upper bound" means some natural number slips past it.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because $u-1$ is below the ceiling, at least one real-life counting number $m$ has already marched past $u-1$.

rungs.why: But $\mathbb{N}$ is closed under $+1$ (Inductive Property), so $m+1$ is also a natural number — and it beats $u$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: But counting never stops! Since $m$ exists, taking one more step to $m+1$ is still a valid counting number, and it catapults right over the supposed maximum ceiling $u$.

rungs.why: This contradicts step 2: $u$ was supposed to be an upper bound of $\mathbb{N}$, yet $m+1\in\mathbb{N}$ exceeds it.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The ceiling failed to hold back the very numbers it claimed to cap. The assumption was impossible—no real number can ever bottle up the natural numbers.

rungs.why: Assume without loss of generality $x > 0$ (if $x \le 0$, shift by an integer). Since $y - x > 0$, Corollary 2.4.5 supplies a denominator $n$.
rungs.m: $$y - x > 0 \implies \exists\, n \in \mathbb{N}: \frac{1}{n} < y - x \iff nx + 1 < ny$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We choose a ruler with tick marks spaced by tiny steps $1/n$, where each step is strictly narrower than the gap between $x$ and $y$.

rungs.why: Apply Corollary 2.4.6 to $nx > 0$ to get the integer $m$ just above $nx$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If we magnify the picture by multiplying by $n$, the left endpoint $nx$ sits just behind some integer $m$.

rungs.why: From $m - 1 \le nx$, we have $m \le nx + 1$. Combine with $nx + 1 < ny$.
rungs.m: $$nx < m \le nx + 1 < ny \implies nx < m < ny$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the gap is wider than $1$ on this magnified scale, the next integer step $m$ lands safely inside the gap without jumping over it.

rungs.why: Divide through by $n > 0$ to obtain the desired rational $r = m/n$.
rungs.m: $$x < \frac{m}{n} < y \implies r := \frac{m}{n} \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ with } x < r < y$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Shrinking the picture back down turns the integer $m$ into the fraction $m/n$, perfectly parked between $x$ and $y$.

title: Density of the irrationals in ℝ

rungs.why: Rescale the target gap by the known irrational $\sqrt2$ (Bartle 2.4.7).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We distort the entire target gap by dividing it by the known irrational $\sqrt{2}$, translating our search into a new gap on a shifted scale.

rungs.why: The Density Theorem (rationals dense in $\mathbb{R}$) supplies a rational strictly between these rescaled endpoints; it can be taken nonzero since the gap contains infinitely many rationals.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because rational fractions are dense everywhere, we can easily grab a nonzero fraction $r$ sitting right inside this newly shifted gap.

rungs.why: Multiply back through by $\sqrt2>0$ (positive, so the inequalities survive) to return to the original scale.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We undo the distortion by multiplying back by $\sqrt{2}$, which drops the number $r\sqrt{2}$ squarely back into our original target gap.

rungs.why: Check $z:=r\sqrt2$ is genuinely irrational: a nonzero rational times an irrational is always irrational.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Multiplying a clean nonzero fraction by $\sqrt{2}$ guarantees an irrational result, giving us the exact irrational stepping stone we needed.

rungs.why: Bounded case: name the infimum and supremum; this immediately traps $S$ inside $[a,b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We locate the absolute lowest floor $a$ and highest ceiling $b$ of the set, so all members of $S$ are trapped between them.

rungs.why: Take any $z$ strictly between $a$ and $b$. Since $a$ is the GREATEST lower bound, anything bigger than it fails to be a lower bound — so some point of $S$ sits below $z$; symmetrically for $b$ and a point above $z$.
rungs.m: $$a < z<b \ \Rightarrow\ \exists x\in S: x < z, \quad \exists y\in S: z < y$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Any point $z$ inside the floor and ceiling is not alone: there is guaranteed to be an element of $S$ to its left and another element of $S$ to its right.

rungs.why: Now $x < z< y$ with $x,y\in S$ — the hypothesis (property (1)) forces the WHOLE segment $[x,y]$, including $z$, into $S$.
rungs.m: $$x < z< y,\ x,y\in S \ \Rightarrow\ z\in[x,y]\subseteq S$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because $S$ has no internal gaps, the entire solid bridge between the left point and right point belongs to $S$, automatically swallowing $z$.

rungs.why: $z$ was an arbitrary point of $(a,b)$, so the whole open interval sits inside $S$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because this works for every single interior point, every scrap of space between $a$ and $b$ is solidly packed into $S$.

rungs.why: Combine with $S\subseteq[a,b]$ from step 1; whether the endpoints $a,b$ themselves belong to $S$ determines which of the four interval types $S$ is.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The entire body of the interval is present; the only open question is whether the two outer boundary posts are included or left out.

rungs.why: Collect all left endpoints into one set; nestedness ($I_n\subseteq I_1$) makes $b_1$ an upper bound for the whole set.
rungs.m: $$\{a_n : n\in\mathbb{N}\}, \qquad a_n\le b_1 \ \text{ for all } n$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We gather all the left endpoints together; because every nested box sits inside the very first box, the right wall of the first box caps them all.

rungs.why: The set of left endpoints is nonempty and bounded above, so Completeness hands us its supremum.
rungs.m: $$\xi := \sup\{a_n : n\in\mathbb{N}\} \ \text{ exists}, \qquad a_n\le\xi\ \text{ for all } n$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: As the left walls push forward without escaping the ceiling, completeness guarantees they converge on an ultimate rightmost frontier point $\xi$.

rungs.why: Fix one index $n$ and show $b_n$ is an upper bound for EVERY $a_k$ — split into two cases by which interval nests inside which.
rungs.m: $$\text{if } n\le k: I_k\subseteq I_n \Rightarrow a_k\le b_k\le b_n; \qquad \text{if } k < n: I_n\subseteq I_k \Rightarrow a_k\le a_n\le b_n$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Russian nesting dolls never cross walls: no left wall from any box can ever stick out past the right wall of any other box.

rungs.why: Either way $a_k\le b_n$ for every $k$, so $b_n$ is an upper bound of the whole set of left endpoints — hence at least as big as the LEAST such bound, $\xi$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Since right wall $b_n$ stays to the right of all left walls, it must also stay to the right of their ultimate frontier point $\xi$.

rungs.why: This held for every $n$, so $\xi$ sits between each interval's own two endpoints.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The special point $\xi$ is permanently pinned between the left wall and right wall of every single box in the entire infinite chain.

rungs.why: That is exactly membership in every $I_n$ simultaneously.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: This point $\xi$ survives inside all the infinitely nested boxes at once—their shared intersection is never empty.

title: Nested Intervals Theorem: Uniqueness of Common Point

rungs.why: From the proof of 2.5.2, $\xi = \sup\{a_n\}$ and $\eta = \inf\{b_n\}$ satisfy $\xi \le \eta$, and $x \in \bigcap I_n \iff \xi \le x \le \eta$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Any point surviving in all boxes is trapped between the frontier of all left walls $\xi$ and the frontier of all right walls $\eta$.

rungs.why: Subtract the inequalities to bound the gap $\eta - \xi$ by the length of $I_n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The distance between these two frontiers cannot be any wider than the width of the containing box.

rungs.why: Since $\inf\{b_n - a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} = 0$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $b_m - a_m < \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the boxes shrink down to zero size, the gap between $\xi$ and $\eta$ can be made smaller than any positive margin you can name.

rungs.why: By Theorem 2.1.9 (Positive Margin Property), $0 \le \eta - \xi < \varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon > 0$ forces $\eta - \xi = 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Two fixed points separated by less than any positive distance must be the exact same point; the collapsing walls isolate a single unique number.

title: Uncountability of ℝ (Cantor Nested Intervals Proof)

rungs.why: Assume for contradiction that $I = [0, 1]$ is countable; enumerate it completely.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We test what happens if someone claims to possess a complete, numbered roll call containing every single real number between $0$ and $1$.

rungs.why: Divide $[0, 1]$ into three equal subintervals $[0, 1/3], [1/3, 2/3], [2/3, 1]$. At least one subinterval does not contain $x_1$; call it $I_1 = [a_1, b_1]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We chop the interval into three thirds; since person $x_1$ can only be in one place, we pick a closed third that completely shuts out $x_1$.

rungs.why: Inductively, given $I_k$, divide it into three subintervals. At least one does not contain $x_{k+1}$; call it $I_{k+1}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Step by step, we zoom into smaller nested rooms, each deliberately constructed to lock out the next person on the list.

rungs.why: This produces a nested sequence of nonempty closed bounded intervals $I_1 \supseteq I_2 \supseteq \cdots$. By Nested Intervals (2.5.2), a common point exists.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The Nested Intervals Property guarantees that there is at least one survivor point $\xi$ sitting at the very center of all these nested rooms.

rungs.why: Since $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n$, and $x_n \notin I_n$, $\xi$ cannot equal $x_n$ for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: This survivor $\xi$ was locked out of person $n$'s room for every $n$, so $\xi$ is not on the list at all! The master list was incomplete, proving real numbers can never be counted.

rungs.why: Apply the definition of convergence with the specific tolerance $\varepsilon=1$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We draw a simple safety bubble of radius $1$ around the limit destination $x$; eventually, the infinite tail steps inside and stays there.

rungs.why: Triangle inequality turns "close to $x$" into an explicit numerical bound on $|x_n|$ itself, for the tail.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Since all late terms stay within $1$ unit of $x$, none can stray farther from zero than the distance to $x$ plus $1$.

rungs.why: The finitely many terms before index $K$ form a finite set, automatically bounded — take the largest of them, together with the tail bound.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Before entering the safety bubble, only a finite number of early terms can wander wild; we simply look through them all and find the single largest value.

rungs.why: Every term, early or late, is now controlled by the same single number $M$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: With the early wild terms and the late settled tail both accounted for, the entire infinite sequence is securely caged inside $[-M, M]$.

title: Limit Theorems: Algebra of Limits for Sequences

rungs.why: (Sum) Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $K_1, K_2$ for $\varepsilon/2$ bounds on $x_n$ and $y_n$. For $n \ge K = \max\{K_1, K_2\}$:
rungs.meaning: What this really means: To keep the combined error below $\varepsilon$, we split the allowed error in half, requiring each sequence to stay within $\varepsilon/2$ of its own limit.

rungs.why: (Product) Rewrite the error by inserting and subtracting $x_n y$:
rungs.m: $$|x_n y_n - xy| = |x_n(y_n - y) + y(x_n - x)| \le |x_n||y_n - y| + |y||x_n - x|$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We express product error as a combination of $y_n$'s error and $x_n$'s error, each multiplied by the size of the accompanying term.

rungs.why: By Theorem 3.2.2, $(x_n)$ is bounded: $|x_n| \le M$. Set $M' = \max\{M, |y|\} > 0$. Choose indices so $|y_n - y| < \varepsilon/(2M')$ and $|x_n - x| < \varepsilon/(2M')$.
rungs.m: $$|x_n y_n - xy| \le M'|y_n - y| + M'|x_n - x| < M'\frac{\varepsilon}{2M'} + M'\frac{\varepsilon}{2M'} = \varepsilon$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because convergent sequences never blow up to infinity, their multipliers stay safely capped, allowing us to crush the product error below $\varepsilon$.

rungs.why: (Quotient) Since $z \ne 0$, set $\alpha = |z|/2 > 0$. Past some $K_1$, $|z_n - z| < \alpha \implies |z_n| > |z|/2$. Then:
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We ensure the denominator $z_n$ never ventures dangerously close to zero, so taking reciprocals cannot trigger an explosion to infinity.

rungs.why: Apply the product rule to $x_n \cdot (1/z_n)$ to finish.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Since division is just multiplying by a reciprocal, the quotient limit is handed to us directly by the product rule.

rungs.why: Suppose for contradiction the limit $x$ is negative; turn the gap into a tolerance.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We test the absurd scenario where a stream of nonnegative numbers allegedly converges to a strictly negative target $x$, measuring the gap from $x$ up to zero.

rungs.why: Convergence traps all sufficiently late terms within $\varepsilon$ of $x$.
rungs.m: $$\exists K:\ n\ge K \Rightarrow x-\varepsilon < x_n < x+\varepsilon$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: By definition of convergence, the numbers must eventually bunch tightly inside a small personal bubble around this negative target.

rungs.why: The right-hand bound, with this particular $\varepsilon$, collapses to exactly $0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: But this bubble lies entirely in negative territory—even its highest ceiling fails to reach zero.

rungs.why: So some term (e.g. $x_K$) is strictly negative — contradicting the hypothesis that $x_n\ge0$ for all $n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: That forces sequence terms to be negative, flatly contradicting that every term was nonnegative from the start.

title: Convergent sequences inherit their bounds in the limit

rungs.why: Shift so the lower bound becomes a nonnegativity statement.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We measure every term relative to the lower bound $a$, converting the question into a stream of nonnegative clearances above the floor.

rungs.why: Apply the nonnegativity-passes-to-the-limit result (c.3.2.4) to $(y_n)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Since clearances above $a$ are always nonnegative, their final limit must be nonnegative too, keeping the limit at or above $a$.

rungs.why: Symmetrically, shift so the upper bound becomes a nonnegativity statement.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We do the exact same check from the ceiling, measuring the remaining headroom down to $x_n$ as a nonnegative quantity.

rungs.why: Apply c.3.2.4 again, to $(z_n)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Nonnegative headroom means the limit cannot puncture the ceiling $b$, locking the limit inside the original fences $[a, b]$.

rungs.why: Name the common limit of the two outer sequences.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Both the lower and upper guard sequences are heading toward the exact same destination $w$.

rungs.why: Given $\varepsilon>0$, both outer convergences supply an index past which they are within $\varepsilon$ of $w$ — take the larger of the two indices.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: After a certain point, both guards are guaranteed to enter a narrow corridor of width $\varepsilon$ around the target $w$.

rungs.why: Shift the squeeze hypothesis $x_n\le y_n\le z_n$ by subtracting $w$ from every term.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We center our view on the destination $w$ to observe the relative distances of all three sequences.

rungs.why: For $n\ge K$ the outer two shifted terms are trapped in $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$, so the middle one is squeezed into the same interval.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the middle sequence is trapped between the two guards, it is physically compressed into that same corridor with nowhere to run.

rungs.why: That is exactly $|y_n-w|<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge K$, with the same $K$ working for every $\varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The middle sequence is forced to converge to the exact same target $w$.

title: The square-root function preserves sequence limits

rungs.why: By c.3.2.4, the limit itself is nonnegative, so $\sqrt{x}$ makes sense to begin with.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because nonnegativity survives into the limit, the destination $x$ cannot be negative, ensuring $\sqrt{x}$ is a valid real number.

rungs.why: Case $x=0$: given $\varepsilon>0$, convergence traps $x_n$ below $\varepsilon^2$ eventually.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: When heading to zero, asking $\sqrt{x_n}$ to stay within $\varepsilon$ is the same as asking $x_n$ to stay within $\varepsilon^2$, which standard convergence easily delivers.

rungs.why: Taking square roots (an increasing operation on nonnegatives) gives exactly the $\varepsilon$-bound needed.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Taking square roots immediately verifies that $\sqrt{x_n}$ is within $\varepsilon$ of zero, proving convergence for the zero case.

rungs.why: Case $x>0$: multiply and divide by the conjugate to turn a difference of square roots into a controlled multiple of $|x_n-x|$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: When the limit is positive, the difference-of-squares trick turns a tricky difference of square roots into the familiar difference $|x_n - x|$.

rungs.why: The denominator is bounded below by $\sqrt{x}>0$ (dropping the nonnegative $\sqrt{x_n}$ only shrinks the denominator, making the fraction bigger), which is what makes the division safe.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The denominator never drops below $\sqrt{x}$, which acts as a safety shield preventing the fraction from ever blowing up.

rungs.why: The right-hand side shrinks to $0$ because $x_n\to x$, and a constant multiple of something shrinking to $0$ still shrinks to $0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: As $x_n$ approaches $x$, the gap vanishes, dragging the difference between their square roots down to zero as well.

rungs.why: (⇒) If $X$ converges it is automatically bounded — already established.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Any journey that settles at a finite destination must stay within a bounded territory.

rungs.why: (⇐) Now suppose $X=(x_n)$ is bounded AND increasing; Completeness hands us a candidate limit — the supremum of the whole set of terms.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If a sequence marches steadily upward against a ceiling, completeness guarantees there is an exact, absolute lowest ceiling $x^*$.

rungs.why: Given $\varepsilon>0$, $x^\ast-\varepsilon$ is too small to be an upper bound (it is strictly below the LEAST upper bound), so some particular term beats it.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If you step back slightly from the ceiling by any margin $\varepsilon$, at least one scout term $x_K$ has already marched past that line.

rungs.why: Monotonicity (increasing) means every later term is at least as large as $x_K$, so it inherits the same lower bound.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the sequence never backtracks, all subsequent terms are permanently locked in ahead of that scout term.

rungs.why: Combine with $x_n\le x^\ast$ (since $x^\ast$ is an upper bound of every term) to trap $x_n$ in a shrinking band around $x^\ast$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: All late terms are trapped between the scout's mark and the ceiling itself, compressed into a narrow band of width $\varepsilon$.

rungs.why: That is exactly $|x_n-x^\ast|<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge K$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because this squeeze holds for any tolerance $\varepsilon$, the sequence undeniably converges to the ceiling $x^*$.

rungs.why: Decreasing case is free: negate the sequence to flip it into an increasing one, apply the increasing case, then flip signs back — exactly the trick used for the infimum half of Completeness (c.2.3.6).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Stepping downward against a floor is simply stepping upward on a flipped mirror world, giving us the decreasing case for free.

title: The Number e via the Monotone Convergence Theorem

rungs.why: Expand $e_n = (1 + 1/n)^n$ using the Binomial Theorem.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We break open the compounding growth formula using the binomial expansion to inspect every piece of interest earned.

rungs.why: Simplify each binomial coefficient by dividing powers of $n$ into each linear factor.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Writing each term cleanly reveals that larger compounding frequency $n$ reduces the shrinkage factors, making every piece bigger.

rungs.why: Compare $e_n$ with $e_{n+1}$: the expansion of $e_{n+1}$ has one extra positive term, and each factor $(1 - k/(n+1)) > (1 - k/n)$ is strictly larger. Thus $e_n < e_{n+1}$.
rungs.m: $$e_n < e_{n+1} \quad \text{for all } n \in \mathbb{N} \implies (e_n) \text{ is strictly increasing}$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Compounding more often increases the size of every existing piece and adds a brand-new positive piece, so the total always grows.

rungs.why: To find an upper bound, observe that $(1 - k/n) < 1$ for all $k \ge 1$. Replace every parenthesized factor by $1$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If we generously drop all the shrinkage factors and round them up to $1$, we obtain an easy-to-analyze upper ceiling.

rungs.why: Since $k! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdots k \ge 2^{k-1}$ for $k \ge 2$, we have $\frac{1}{k!} \le \frac{1}{2^{k-1}}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Factorials grow faster than powers of $2$, so their reciprocals shrink faster than powers of $1/2$.

rungs.why: Sum the geometric series: $1 + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{2^{n-1}} = \frac{1 - (1/2)^n}{1 - 1/2} < 2$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Summing those powers of $1/2$ never even reaches $2$, so the entire compounding sequence is capped strictly below $3$.

rungs.why: Since $(e_n)$ is increasing and bounded above by $3$, the Monotone Convergence Theorem (3.3.2) proves that the limit exists.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because compounding climbs steadily without ever breaching $3$, it is mathematically guaranteed to lock onto a precise limit: Euler's number $e$.

rungs.why: (⇒) Suppose $X$ converges to $x$; split an arbitrary tolerance in half, one half for each of two indices being compared.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If terms converge to a target $x$, late terms must huddle within $\varepsilon/2$ of that target.

rungs.why: For any two indices $n,m$ past $K$, route the comparison between $x_n$ and $x_m$ through the shared point $x$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Two runners who are both within half a mile of the finish line cannot be more than a mile apart from each other.

rungs.why: (⇐) Now suppose $X$ is Cauchy. First show it is bounded: fix $\varepsilon=1$; the tail is trapped within $1$ of a single reference term $x_H$, and finitely many earlier terms are trivially bounded.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If terms bunch together, they cannot drift off to infinity; anchoring them to one late term cages the entire sequence.

rungs.why: So $X$ is bounded — Bolzano–Weierstrass now supplies a convergent SUBsequence, with some limit $x^\ast$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the sequence is bounded, a sub-stream of terms is guaranteed to zoom in on an accumulation point $x^*$.

rungs.why: Given $\varepsilon>0$, use the Cauchy property (with margin $\varepsilon/2$) to trap ALL sufficiently late terms close to each other.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The Cauchy property guarantees that all late terms in the sequence are tightly grouped together like a flock of birds.

rungs.why: Pick one subsequence index $K$ that is both past $H(\varepsilon/2)$ and close enough to $x^\ast$ (possible since the subsequence itself converges to $x^\ast$).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We grab one member of the flock that is already within $\varepsilon/2$ of the target destination $x^*$.

rungs.why: Route ANY term $x_n$ (with $n\ge H(\varepsilon/2)$) through this anchor $x_K$ via the triangle inequality.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the whole flock stays close to that anchor, and the anchor is close to $x^*$, the entire flock is dragged into $x^*$, proving full convergence.

title: Contractive Sequences: Convergence and Error Estimates

rungs.why: Apply the contractive condition repeatedly back to the first step.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Each step shrinks by a factor of $C < 1$, so step sizes decrease exponentially fast compared to the initial step.

rungs.why: For $m > n$, expand $|x_m - x_n|$ by adding and subtracting intermediate terms and applying the triangle inequality.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The total distance between term $n$ and any future term $m$ is bounded by the sum of each intermediate hop.

rungs.why: Substitute the geometric bounds for each consecutive difference.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We replace each hop with its geometric bound, factoring out the shrinkage factor $C^{n-1}$ from the starting gap.

rungs.why: Sum the finite geometric series: $1 + C + \cdots + C^{m-n-1} < \frac{1}{1 - C}$ since $0 < C < 1$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Even if you walk infinitely many hops into the future, the sum of shrinking steps is safely capped by a convergent geometric series.

rungs.why: Since $0 < C < 1$, $\lim_{n\to\infty} C^{n-1} = 0$. Hence $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence, and by Theorem 3.5.5 it converges to some limit $x^*$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because $C^{n-1}$ shrinks to zero, late terms are pinned so closely together that the sequence is Cauchy, guaranteeing it converges.

rungs.why: Take ANY sequence $(x_n)$ in $A\setminus\{c\}$ with $x_n\to c$; by the Sequential Criterion, both image sequences converge to the function limits.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We test the functions along any stream of stepping stones approaching $c$; their outputs are guaranteed to march toward $L$ and $M$.

rungs.why: This is now purely a statement about SEQUENCES — apply the already-known algebra of limits for convergent sequences termwise.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Now that we are dealing with standard sequences, all the arithmetic rules we already proved for sequences click right into place.

rungs.why: But $\big((f+g)(x_n)\big)=\big(f(x_n)+g(x_n)\big)$ by the very DEFINITION of the sum of two functions.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Evaluating the combined function $(f+g)$ at each stepping stone is by definition just adding the two outputs together.

rungs.why: This held for an ARBITRARY sequence $(x_n)\to c$ in $A\setminus\{c\}$ — exactly the hypothesis of the Sequential Criterion, applied in the other direction.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because this works for every possible path of stepping stones approaching $c$, no path can ever miss the target $L+M$.

rungs.why: So the Sequential Criterion (c.4.1.8) hands back a genuine function limit; the product, difference, scalar-multiple, and (when $H\ne0$) quotient rules follow the identical pattern.
rungs.m: $$\lim_{x\to c}(f+g)=L+M \quad(\text{similarly for } f-g,\ fg,\ bf,\ f/h)$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The sequential bridge converts our sequence result into an airtight proof for the function limit itself.

rungs.why: Let $(x_n)$ be an arbitrary sequence in $A \setminus \{c\}$ such that $(x_n) \to c$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We pick any path of stepping stones heading toward $c$ without ever landing on $c$.

rungs.why: By the Sequential Criterion (4.1.8), since $\lim_{x\to c} f = L$ and $\lim_{x\to c} h = L$, the image sequences converge.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Along this path, the lower guard function and upper guard function both approach the exact same value $L$.

rungs.why: The sandwich inequality holds for every term: $f(x_n) \le g(x_n) \le h(x_n)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: At every step of the journey, the values of $g$ remain trapped between the two guards.

rungs.why: Apply the Squeeze Theorem for sequences (Theorem 3.2.7) to $(f(x_n)), (g(x_n)), (h(x_n))$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The already-proven sequence Squeeze Theorem crushes the middle values into the shared target $L$.

rungs.why: Since this holds for every such sequence $(x_n)$, the Sequential Criterion guarantees that $\lim_{x\to c} g(x) = L$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because every sequence path yields $L$, the function $g(x)$ itself is forced to converge to $L$.

rungs.why: (⇒) Assume $\lim_{x\to c} f = L$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $0 < |x-c| < \delta$ ($x \in A$) implies $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If the two-sided limit exists, there is a circular safety zone around $c$ where outputs stay within $\varepsilon$ of $L$ on both sides.

rungs.why: If $x \in A$ and $0 < x - c < \delta$, then $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, so $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$. Hence $\lim_{x\to c^+} f = L$. Similarly for $x < c$, $\lim_{x\to c^-} f = L$.
rungs.m: $$\lim_{x\to c^+} f = L \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x\to c^-} f = L$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Since the safety zone covers all nearby points, it automatically covers points approaching strictly from the right and strictly from the left.

rungs.why: (⇐) Assume $\lim_{x\to c^+} f = L$ and $\lim_{x\to c^-} f = L$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, obtain $\delta_1 > 0$ for the right side and $\delta_2 > 0$ for the left side.
rungs.m: $$0 < x - c < \delta_1 \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon, \qquad 0 < c - x < \delta_2 \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Approaching from the right offers a safety distance $\delta_1$, while approaching from the left offers a safety distance $\delta_2$.

rungs.why: Define $\delta := \min\{\delta_1, \delta_2\} > 0$. If $x \in A$ satisfies $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, then either $0 < x - c < \delta \le \delta_1$ or $0 < c - x < \delta \le \delta_2$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We choose the smaller of the two distances, so anyone within $\delta$ of $c$ is protected no matter which side they come from.

rungs.why: In either case, $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$. Thus $\lim_{x\to c} f = L$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because both sides merge smoothly at $L$ under the unified buffer $\delta$, the full two-sided limit is established.

rungs.why: Let $\alpha > 0$ be an arbitrary positive real number (if $\alpha \le 0$, any $\delta > 0$ works since $1/x^2 > 0 \ge \alpha$).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Someone challenges us with a towering ceiling $\alpha$ and dares us to prove that the function shoots above it.

rungs.why: Choose $\delta := \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha}} > 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We calculate how close to zero we must stand so that squaring and inverting will surpass that ceiling.

rungs.why: Assume $x$ satisfies $0 < |x - 0| < \delta$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We step inside this designated safety window around zero.

rungs.why: Square both sides (both are positive, so the inequality preserves order).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because $x$ is so tiny, squaring it compresses it into an even tinier fraction, strictly below $1/\alpha$.

rungs.why: Take the reciprocal of both sides, which reverses the inequality.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Dividing $1$ by this microscopic fraction launches the result skyward, soaring past the target ceiling $\alpha$.

rungs.why: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be given.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Someone specifies a tiny error band $\varepsilon$ around zero and asks how far right we must travel before $1/x$ enters that band.

rungs.why: Choose the horizon $K := \frac{1}{\varepsilon} > 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We set our horizon marker $K$ at $1/\varepsilon$; stepping past this point ensures the reciprocal drops below $\varepsilon$.

rungs.why: Assume $x \in (0, \infty)$ satisfies $x > K$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: We travel beyond this horizon marker into the distant positive territory.

rungs.why: Take reciprocals, noting that both sides are positive.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Inverting larger numbers yields smaller fractions, pushing $1/x$ safely underneath $\varepsilon$.

rungs.why: Translate this into the absolute value distance to 0.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The distance between $1/x$ and zero is strictly within the required tolerance $\varepsilon$, proving that $1/x$ vanishes at infinity.

rungs.why: Suppose for contradiction that $S \ne \mathbb{N}$, and let $E$ be the set of elements not in $S$.
rungs.m: What this really means: We imagine that some natural numbers fail the statement, and gather all these failing numbers into a basket $E$ to find the very first failure.

rungs.why: By the Well-Ordering Property of $\mathbb{N}$, every non-empty subset of natural numbers has a least element $m$.
rungs.m: What this really means: Natural numbers have a hard bottom floor at $1$; you cannot count down forever. So among all the failures in our basket, there MUST be an absolute first, smallest failure $m$.

rungs.why: Since hypothesis (1) gives $1 \in S$, $m$ cannot be $1$, so $m > 1$ and $m - 1 \in \mathbb{N}$.
rungs.m: What this really means: Because $1$ was already verified to work, our first failure cannot be $1$. That means there is an actual positive integer $m - 1$ standing right before it.

rungs.why: Because $m$ is the least element of $E$, the strictly smaller number $m - 1$ cannot belong to $E$, hence $m - 1 \in S$.
rungs.m: What this really means: Because $m$ was the very FIRST failure, the number directly before it ($m - 1$) was completely innocent and passed the test successfully.

rungs.why: By hypothesis (2), since $m - 1 \in S$, the successor $(m - 1) + 1 = m$ must also belong to $S$, contradicting $m \in E$.
rungs.m: What this really means: But the induction rule says whenever a number passes, the next number must pass too! So $m$ must pass, contradicting that it failed. Thus, no failures ever existed!

rungs.why: Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a subset that has no least element. We will prove $S = \emptyset$.
rungs.m: What this really means: We test what happens if a set of natural numbers claims to have no smallest member; we show such a set cannot even contain a single element.

rungs.why: Define $T = \mathbb{N} \setminus S$. We show $T = \mathbb{N}$ using induction. First, $1 \in T$, because if $1 \in S$, $1$ would be the least element of $S$ (since $1 \le s$ for all $s \in \mathbb{N}$).
rungs.m: What this really means: The number $1$ is the absolute smallest natural number. If $1$ were allowed into $S$, it would instantly be the minimum; so $1$ is barred from $S$.

rungs.why: Assume ${1, 2, \ldots, k} \subseteq T$. Then no number $\le k$ belongs to $S$.
rungs.m: What this really means: By assuming all numbers up to $k$ are barred from $S$, we know $S$ cannot start anywhere at or below $k$.

rungs.why: If $k + 1 \in S$, then $k + 1$ would be smaller than all other elements of $S$, making it the least element of $S$, a contradiction. Thus $k + 1 \in T$.
rungs.m: What this really means: Now $k+1$ is next. If $k+1$ were in $S$, it would be smaller than everything else left in $S$, making it the least element! To avoid having a minimum, $S$ must shut out $k+1$ as well.

rungs.why: By induction, $T = \mathbb{N}$, which forces $S = \emptyset$.
rungs.m: What this really means: Domino effect! Every single natural number is banned from $S$, leaving $S$ completely empty.

rungs.why: Define $T = \{k \in \mathbb{N} : \{1, 2, \ldots, k\} \subseteq S\}$.
rungs.m: What this really means: Instead of tracking single dominoes, we redefine success as having the entire block of dominoes from $1$ up to $k$ knocked down.

rungs.why: Base step: Since $1 \in S$ by hypothesis (1), $\{1\} \subseteq S$, so $1 \in T$.
rungs.m: What this really means: The very first domino $1$ falls on its own as the base starting push.

rungs.why: Inductive step: Assume $k \in T$. Then $\{1, \ldots, k\} \subseteq S$.
rungs.m: What this really means: We assume that the entire unbroken chain from $1$ all the way to $k$ has successfully fallen.

rungs.why: By hypothesis (2), this implies $k + 1 \in S$. Combining $\{1, \ldots, k\} \subseteq S$ and $k + 1 \in S$ gives $\{1, \ldots, k+1\} \subseteq S$.
rungs.m: What this really means: Because the entire previous history is solid, the rule kicks the very next domino $k+1$ down, expanding our unbroken fallen chain to length $k+1$.

rungs.why: By standard induction (1.2.1), $T = \mathbb{N}$. Since $k \in T \implies k \in S$, we have $S = \mathbb{N}$.
rungs.m: What this really means: Regular induction now carries our unbroken chain to infinity, proving strong induction is just standard induction in disguise.

title: Countability of Rationals and Uncountability of Reals

rungs.why: Arrange positive rationals $p/q$ in an array with row $p$ and column $q$, and traverse finite diagonals $p + q = k$.
rungs.m: What this really means: Lay every fraction out on a 2D grid and walk across it in diagonal zig-zags so no fraction is stranded infinitely far away.

rungs.why: Omit fractions not in lowest terms. This yields a surjection from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{Q}^+$, proving $\mathbb{Q}^+$ is countable.
rungs.m: What this really means: Cross out duplicates like $2/2$ or $2/4$. Every remaining fraction gets a finite queue number, proving fractions can be counted in line.

rungs.why: Since $\mathbb{Q} = \mathbb{Q}^+ \cup \{0\} \cup (-\mathbb{Q}^+)$ is a union of three countable sets, $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable.
rungs.m: What this really means: Adding negative fractions and zero is just combining three countable lines together, which remains countable.

rungs.why: For $[0, 1]$, assume for contradiction that an enumeration $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ exists. Write each in decimal expansion: $x_n = 0.d_{n1}d_{n2}d_{n3}\ldots$
rungs.m: What this really means: To test if real numbers can also be listed, we pretend an infinite master table contains every single decimal between $0$ and $1$.

rungs.why: Construct $y = 0.y_1 y_2 y_3 \ldots \in [0, 1]$ by choosing $y_n = 2$ if $d_{nn} = 1$, and $y_n = 1$ if $d_{nn} \ne 1$.
rungs.m: What this really means: Cantor looks down the diagonal of the list and flips each digit: the new number intentionally disagrees with the 1st number at digit 1, the 2nd at digit 2, and so on.

rungs.why: Then $y \ne x_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ because their decimal expansions differ at the $n$-th digit, contradicting the enumeration.
rungs.m: What this really means: This new number cannot match ANY number on the entire infinite list because it differs from each by at least one digit! The master list was incomplete.

title: Properties of Countable Sets: Subsets and Unions

rungs.why: Let $S$ be countable and $E \subseteq S$. If $E$ is finite, it is countable. If $E$ is infinite, let $S = \{s_1, s_2, \ldots\}$. Define $n_1$ as the smallest index with $s_{n_1} \in E$.
rungs.m: What this really means: Take your numbered list of items in $S$ and walk down it, picking out the very first item that belongs to your sub-group $E$.

rungs.why: Inductively define $n_k = \min\{j > n_{k-1} : s_j \in E\}$. Then $k \mapsto s_{n_k}$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ to $E$, proving $E$ is countably infinite.
rungs.m: What this really means: Keep walking forward to pick the next member of $E$, renumbering them 1st, 2nd, 3rd. A sub-list of a countable list is always countable.

rungs.why: For the union $A = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n$, list each set: $A_n = \{a_{n1}, a_{n2}, a_{n3}, \ldots\}$. Arrange into a 2D array.
rungs.m: What this really means: When combining countably many lists, write List 1 on Row 1, List 2 on Row 2, forming an infinite table.

rungs.why: Traverse the diagonals $D_k = \{a_{ij} : i + j = k\}$ for $k = 2, 3, 4, \ldots$. Each diagonal $D_k$ has at most $k - 1$ elements (finite).
rungs.m: What this really means: Snake through the table along finite diagonal ribbons, ensuring you visit every row and every column in finite time.

rungs.why: Skipping duplicate elements defines a surjection from $\mathbb{N}$ onto $A$, proving $A$ is countable.
rungs.m: What this really means: Skip duplicates along the way. Since every single item across all lists gets a finite ticket number, the combined super-list is countable.

rungs.why: Suppose for contradiction that $f: A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$ is surjective.
rungs.m: What this really means: We assume every possible subset of $A$ can be paired with an element from $A$ with none left out, setting up a trap that will contradict itself.

rungs.why: Define the diagonal subset $D = \{x \in A : x \notin f(x)\}$. Since $D \subseteq A$, $D \in \mathcal{P}(A)$.
rungs.m: What this really means: We build a "rebel club" $D$ of all elements that do NOT belong to their assigned partner set (like the barber who shaves only those who do not shave themselves).

rungs.why: Since $f$ is surjective, there must exist some element $d \in A$ such that $f(d) = D$.
rungs.m: What this really means: If our pairing truly reached every subset, some element $d$ in our set must have been assigned this rebel club $D$ as its partner.

rungs.why: Now ask: does $d$ belong to $D$? By definition of $D$, $d \in D \iff d \notin f(d)$.
rungs.m: What this really means: We test if $d$ is in $D$. But the rule of the rebel club says an element is in $D$ only if it is NOT in its assigned partner set.

rungs.why: Substitute $f(d) = D$ into the equivalence: $d \in D \iff d \notin D$, an outright logical contradiction.
rungs.m: What this really means: Since $d$\'s assigned set is $D$, this means $d$ is in $D$ if and only if $d$ is NOT in $D$! An impossible paradox proving no set can ever be paired with all its subsets.
