Use the variance identity $\sum_{k=0}^n (k - nt)^2 \binom{n}{k} t^k (1-t)^{n-k} = nt(1-t) \le n/4$ to bound terms where $|k/n - t| \ge \delta$.

title: One-Sided Limits of a Monotone Function

rungs.why: Name the candidate limit: since $f$ is increasing, values left of $c$ are bounded above by $f(c)$, so this set has a supremum.
rungs.m: $$L:=\sup\{f(x):x\in I,\,x < c\}$$ (exists, as the set is nonempty and bounded above by $f(c)$)

rungs.why: Given $\varepsilon>0$, $L-\varepsilon$ is not an upper bound of the set, so some point just left of $c$ already gets close to $L$.
Convert this into an $x$-window using monotonicity: any $y$ between $y_\varepsilon$ and $c$ has $f(y)$ trapped between $f(y_\varepsilon)$ and $L$.
rungs.m: set $\delta_\varepsilon:=c-y_\varepsilon>0$; for $y\in I$ with $0 < c-y<\delta_\varepsilon$: $L-\varepsilon < f(y_\varepsilon)\le f(y)\le L$

rungs.why: Read off convergence directly from that squeeze.
This is precisely the definition of the left-hand limit; the right-hand case is symmetric with $\inf$.

title: Continuity Criteria for an Increasing Function

rungs.why: Recall the Chapter 4 fact linking continuity to one-sided limits.
rungs.m: $f$ continuous at $c$ $\iff$ $\lim_{x\to c^-}f=f(c)=\lim_{x\to c^+}f$ — this is (a) $\iff$ (b)

rungs.why: Substitute the explicit values Theorem 5.6.1 gives for those two limits.
Plugging these in turns (b) into (c) with no extra work.
Translate condition (c) of Corollary 5.6.2 into "gap = 0" at an interior point.
rungs.m: for interior $c$: $j_f(c)=\inf\{f(x):x>c\}-\sup\{f(x):x < c\}=0\iff$ (c) of Cor. 5.6.2 $\iff f$ continuous at $c$

rungs.why: Note the jump can never be negative for an increasing function, since the right floor cannot undercut the left ceiling.
At a left endpoint $a\in I$ there is only a right-hand limit to compare against $f(a)$.
rungs.m: $j_f(a):=\lim_{x\to a^+}f-f(a)=0\iff f(a)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f\iff f$ continuous at $a$

rungs.why: The right-endpoint case is symmetric, using only the left-hand limit.

title: Monotone Functions Have Countably Many Discontinuities

rungs.why: For any finitely many ordered points, their jumps add up to at most the total rise of $f$ across $I$ — the jumps cannot overlap.
rungs.m: for $a\le x_1 < x_2<\cdots < x_n\le b$: $j_f(x_1)+j_f(x_2)+\cdots+j_f(x_n)\le f(b)-f(a)$

rungs.why: Turn "total jump is bounded" into "few big jumps": if more than $k$ points had jump $\ge(f(b)-f(a))/k$, their sum alone would exceed the total rise.
rungs.m: for fixed $k\in\mathbb N$, the set $\{x\in I: j_f(x)\ge (f(b)-f(a))/k\}$ has at most $k$ points

rungs.why: Every discontinuity has strictly positive jump (5.6.3), so $D$ is exactly the union of these threshold sets over all $k$.
A countable union of finite sets is countable.
rungs.m: $D$ is a countable union of finite sets $\implies D$ is countable

rungs.why: Confirm the setup: $J$ is an interval (so it makes sense to ask if $g$ is continuous "at a point of $J$"), and $g$ exists because $f$ is injective.
rungs.m: $J:=f(I)$ is an interval (Thm 5.3.10, since $f$ is continuous on interval $I$); $f$ strictly increasing $\implies$ injective on $I$ $\implies$ $g:J\to\mathbb R$ with $g(f(x))=x$ exists

rungs.why: Show $g$ inherits the order: a bigger output of $f$ must come from a bigger input.
rungs.m: for $y_1 < y_2$ in $J$, write $y_1=f(x_1),\,y_2=f(x_2)$; if $x_1\ge x_2$ then $f(x_1)\ge f(x_2)$, contradicting $y_1 < y_2$ — so $x_1 < x_2$, i.e. $g(y_1) < g(y_2)$

rungs.why: Suppose for contradiction $g$ is discontinuous at some $c\in J$; by 5.6.3 this means a nonzero jump.
rungs.m: suppose $g$ discontinuous at $c\in J$; by Thm 5.6.3, $\lim_{y\to c^-}g<\lim_{y\to c^+}g$

rungs.why: Pick a candidate value strictly between those two one-sided limits of $g$.
rungs.m: choose $x$ with $\lim_{y\to c^-}g < x<\lim_{y\to c^+}g$ and $x\ne g(c)$

rungs.why: Strict monotonicity of $g$ rules out any $y\in J$ actually attaining this $x$ as $g(y)$.
But $x$ sits strictly between values that are limits of points of $I$, so $x$ ought to be trapped inside $I$ — contradicting that $I$ is an interval.
rungs.m: $x\notin I$ contradicts $I$ being an interval, since $x$ lies between elements of $g(J)=I$

title: Rational Powers Commute with nth Roots

rungs.why: Set up the candidate value from the definition of rational powers (5.6.6).
Recall the defining property of the $n$th root: raising it to the $n$th power returns $x$.
Compute $y^n$ using only integer-exponent power laws, reordering the two exponents.
"$y>0$ and $y^n=x^m$" is precisely what it means to say $y$ is the $n$th root of $x^m$.
For $x \ne c$, factor the change in $f$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Express the total vertical jump between the two points as their average slope multiplied by the horizontal step.

rungs.why: Take the limit as $x \to c$ of both sides.
rungs.m: $$\lim_{x\to c}(f(x) - f(c)) = \lim_{x\to c}\left(\frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}\right) \cdot \lim_{x\to c}(x - c)$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: As the two points merge together, the overall gap splits cleanly into the limiting slope times the vanishing step size.

rungs.why: Evaluate the limits: the difference quotient is $f'(c)$, and $(x - c) \to 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Multiplying a finite, well-behaved slope by a step size that shrinks to zero completely crushes the vertical gap to zero.

rungs.why: Conclude that the limit of $f(x)$ equals $f(c)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the gap vanishes entirely, the curve cannot tear or jump, guaranteeing that the function is continuous.

title: Algebraic Properties of Derivatives: Sum, Product, and Quotient Rules

rungs.why: Write the difference quotient for $p = fg$ at $c$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Set up the overall rate of change for the product of two functions over a small step.

rungs.why: Add and subtract $f(c)g(x)$ in the numerator.
rungs.m: $$\frac{f(x)g(x) - f(c)g(x) + f(c)g(x) - f(c)g(c)}{x - c} = \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} g(x) + f(c) \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Insert a shared corner state to split the total area expansion of a rectangle into horizontal and vertical edge expansions.

rungs.why: Since $g$ is differentiable at $c$, Theorem 6.1.2 gives $\lim_{x\to c} g(x) = g(c)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the second function is smooth, it cannot abruptly jump, so its value smoothly settles to its starting height.

rungs.why: Apply the limit laws for sums and products.
rungs.m: $$p'(c) = \lim_{x\to c}\left(\frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}\right) \lim_{x\to c} g(x) + f(c) \lim_{x\to c}\left(\frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}\right) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Each individual rate of change pairs naturally with the other function's frozen value, yielding the familiar product rule.

rungs.why: For $q = f/g$, write $(f(x)/g(x) - f(c)/g(c))/(x - c) = \frac{1}{g(x)g(c)} [\frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}g(c) - f(c)\frac{g(x)-g(c)}{x-c}]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Finding a common denominator turns a ratio of changing rates into a cross-difference divided by the squared base.

rungs.why: Verify base step $n=1$: $(x)' = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{(x+h) - x}{h} = 1 = 1 \cdot x^0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The straight line with unit slope changes at an exact one-to-one rate with its input.

rungs.why: Inductive hypothesis: assume $(x^k)' = k x^{k-1}$ for $k \in \mathbb{N}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Assume the power rule holds true for a power of degree $k$ as our induction platform.

rungs.why: Write $x^{k+1} = x \cdot x^k$ and apply the Product Rule (6.1.3).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Splitting the next power into an extra factor of $x$ lets the product rule cleanly combine $1$ copy of $x^k$ with $k$ copies of $x^k$.

rungs.why: By the Principle of Induction (1.2.1), $(x^n)' = n x^{n-1}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The induction dominoes collapse in order, locking the power formula in place for every positive whole number.

rungs.why: For $m = -n$ with $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $x \ne 0$, apply Quotient Rule to $1/x^n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Inverting the function flips the sign of the rate and subtracts one from the power, extending the rule seamlessly to negative integers.

title: Carathéodory’s Theorem and the Chain Rule

rungs.why: Define $\varphi(x) = (f(x) - f(c))/(x - c)$ for $x \ne c$, and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Replace messy division by an auxiliary continuous slope factor that stays well-behaved even at the reference point.

rungs.why: By definition, differentiability of $f$ at $c$ holds iff $\lim_{x\to c} \varphi(x) = f'(c) = \varphi(c)$, which is continuity of $\varphi$ at $c$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Having a well-defined derivative is completely equivalent to this slope helper function connecting continuously without gaps.

rungs.why: For the Chain Rule with $g$ differentiable at $c$, write $g(x) - g(c) = \psi(x)(x - c)$ with $\psi$ continuous at $c$ and $\psi(c) = g'(c)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Apply the exact same smooth-slope factorization to the inner function.

rungs.why: Substitute $g(x)$ into $f$: $f(g(x)) - f(g(c)) = \varphi(g(x))(g(x) - g(c)) = \varphi(g(x))\psi(x)(x - c)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Nesting one function inside the other simply multiplies their two smooth slope factors together without any risk of dividing by zero.

rungs.why: Take the limit as $x \to c$: since $g$ is continuous at $c$, $\varphi(g(x)) \to \varphi(g(c)) = f'(g(c))$ and $\psi(x) \to g'(c)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Taking the limit directly multiplies the outer rate of change by the inner rate of change, proving the chain rule cleanly.

rungs.why: By Carathéodory (6.1.5), $\exists \varphi$ continuous at $c$ with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ and $\varphi(c) = f'(c) \ne 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Represent the original function with its continuous slope factor, which is guaranteed not to vanish at the target point.

rungs.why: Since $\varphi(c) \ne 0$ and $\varphi$ is continuous at $c$, $\varphi(x) \ne 0$ on a neighborhood $V$ of $c$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Continuity preserves the non-zero sign nearby, creating a safe zone where dividing by the slope will never cause a zero error.

rungs.why: For $y \in f(V)$, let $x = g(y)$ and $d = f(c)$. Substitute into Carathéodory's relation.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Translate the relationship into output coordinates through the inverse function.

rungs.why: Divide by $\varphi(g(y))$: $g(y) - g(d) = \frac{1}{\varphi(g(y))} (y - d)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Turning the equation around isolates the step in the inverse function, revealing its slope to be the reciprocal of the original slope.

rungs.why: By Theorem 5.6.5, $g$ is continuous at $d$, so $\lim_{y\to d} g(y) = c$. Therefore $\psi$ is continuous at $d$ with $\psi(d) = 1/\varphi(c) = 1/f'(c)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the inverse function is continuous, its limiting slope is simply the reciprocal of the original curve's slope at that point.

rungs.why: Assume $f$ has a relative maximum at interior point $c$. Then $f(x) \le f(c)$ for all $x \in (c - \delta, c + \delta) \subseteq I$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: At the highest point of a hill, any step in either direction takes you down or keeps you level.

rungs.why: For $x \in (c - \delta, c)$, $x - c < 0$, so the difference quotient is $\ge 0$.
rungs.m: $$\frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} \ge 0 \implies f'(c) = \lim_{x\to c^-} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} \ge 0$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Approaching the summit from the left means you were climbing uphill, so the left-hand slope cannot be negative.

rungs.why: For $x \in (c, c + \delta)$, $x - c > 0$, so the difference quotient is $\le 0$.
rungs.m: $$\frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} \le 0 \implies f'(c) = \lim_{x\to c^+} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} \le 0$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Moving forward past the summit means you are heading downhill, so the right-hand slope cannot be positive.

rungs.why: Since $f$ is differentiable at $c$, both one-sided limits are equal to $f'(c)$, forcing $0 \le f'(c) \le 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The only number that is simultaneously at least zero and at most zero is zero, meaning the tangent line at the peak is perfectly flat.

title: Critical Points and Location of Extrema

rungs.why: Let $c$ be an interior point where $f$ attains a relative extremum.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Start with any peak or trough that sits safely inside the boundaries of the interval.

rungs.why: Case 1: If $f$ is not differentiable at $c$, then $c$ satisfies condition (2).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If the graph forms a sharp corner or kink where no unique tangent line exists, it is instantly cataloged as a critical candidate.

rungs.why: Case 2: If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, apply Fermat’s Interior Extremum Theorem (6.2.1).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If the graph is smooth at the extremum, Fermat forces its tangent line to level off completely, narrowing the search to zero-slope points.

rungs.why: By the Maximum-Minimum Theorem (5.3.4), $f$ attains an absolute maximum $M$ and minimum $m$ on $[a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Any continuous journey on a closed interval must achieve an absolute highest altitude and an absolute lowest altitude.

rungs.why: If $m = M$, then $f$ is constant on $[a, b]$, so $f'(x) = 0$ for all $x \in (a, b)$ and any interior point $c$ works.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If the highest and lowest altitudes are identical, the path was completely flat the whole way, so the slope was zero everywhere.

rungs.why: If $m < M$, then since $f(a) = f(b)$, at least one of $m$ or $M$ must be attained at an interior point $c \in (a, b)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the endpoints start and end at the same level, any climb or dip must turn around somewhere in the middle.

rungs.why: Since $c$ is an interior extremum and $f$ is differentiable on $(a, b)$, Fermat\'s Theorem (6.2.1) ensures $f'(c) = 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: At that internal turnaround peak or valley, the curve is momentarily horizontal, matching the level slope of the endpoints.

rungs.why: Define the auxiliary function measuring vertical distance to the chord.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Tilt the coordinate frame by measuring how far the curve deviates above or below the straight chord connecting its ends.

rungs.why: Evaluate $h$ at the endpoints $a$ and $b$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: At both endpoints, the curve and its connecting chord meet, meaning the tilted error drops to zero at both ends.

rungs.why: Apply Rolle’s Theorem to $h$ on $[a, b]$ to find $c \in (a, b)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: By Rolle's theorem, this tilted loop must reach a maximum deviation where its relative tilt is flat.

rungs.why: Differentiate $h(x)$ and set equal to $0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: A flat relative deviation means the curve's instantaneous tangent is perfectly parallel to the secant chord.

title: Zero Derivative Characterization and Constant Difference

rungs.why: Let $x \in (a, b]$. Apply MVT (6.2.4) to $f$ on the subinterval $[a, x]$.
rungs.m: $$\exists c \in (a, x) : f(x) - f(a) = f'(c)(x - a)$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Connect the starting point to any chosen destination using the Mean Value Theorem.

rungs.why: By hypothesis, $f'(c) = 0$ since $c \in (a, b)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the slope is zero everywhere along the journey, no altitude can ever be gained or lost.

rungs.why: Conclude $f(x) = f(a)$ for all $x \in [a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Having zero speed at every instant forces the position to remain permanently frozen at its initial value.

rungs.why: For (b), define $h(x) = f(x) - g(x)$. Then $h'(x) = f'(x) - g'(x) = 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If two curves always climb at identical speeds, their gap never changes, so they are exact vertical copies of each other.

rungs.why: Let $x_1, x_2 \in [a, b]$ with $x_1 < x_2$. Apply MVT (6.2.4) to $f$ on $[x_1, x_2]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Express the net change between any two points as the instantaneous slope at an intermediate spot multiplied by the distance traveled.

rungs.why: Since $x_2 - x_1 > 0$, if $f'(c) \ge 0$, then $f(x_2) - f(x_1) \ge 0$, so $f(x_1) \le f(x_2)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: A non-negative slope ensures the curve never rolls backward or loses height as you move to the right.

rungs.why: If $f'(c) > 0$, then $f(x_2) - f(x_1) > 0$, so $f(x_1) < f(x_2)$ (strictly increasing).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: A strictly positive slope guarantees the curve is actively climbing uphill at all times.

rungs.why: Conversely, if $f$ is increasing, for any $x \ne c$, $(f(x) - f(c))/(x - c) \ge 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Since secant slopes between points on an uphill climb are always non-negative, their limit can never dip below zero.

title: First Derivative Test for Relative Extrema

rungs.why: Let $x \in (c - \delta, c)$. Apply MVT (6.2.4) on $[x, c]$: $f(c) - f(x) = f'(z_1)(c - x)$ for some $z_1 \in (x, c)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Measure the climb leading up to the candidate peak using the Mean Value Theorem.

rungs.why: Since $f'(z_1) \ge 0$ and $c - x > 0$, $f(c) - f(x) \ge 0 \implies f(x) \le f(c)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the slope was positive leading up to the summit, every point just before it was lower than the summit.

rungs.why: Let $x \in (c, c + \delta)$. Apply MVT on $[c, x]$: $f(x) - f(c) = f'(z_2)(x - c)$ for some $z_2 \in (c, x)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Measure the descent immediately following the candidate peak.

rungs.why: Since $f'(z_2) \le 0$ and $x - c > 0$, $f(x) - f(c) \le 0 \implies f(x) \le f(c)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the slope turns downward right after the summit, every point past it is also lower, crowning that point as a true peak.

title: Mean Value Inequality: Bounded Derivatives Imply Lipschitz Continuity

rungs.why: Let $x, y \in I$ with $x \ne y$. Apply MVT (6.2.4) to $f$ on the interval between $x$ and $y$.
rungs.m: $$\exists c \text{ between } x \text{ and } y : f(x) - f(y) = f'(c)(x - y)$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The Mean Value Theorem equates the overall vertical shift between any two points to the speed at an intermediate point times the distance.

rungs.why: Take the absolute value of both sides.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The magnitude of the output jump is precisely the magnitude of the slope times the input separation.

rungs.why: Apply the hypothesis $|f'(c)| \le M$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: A universal speed limit $M$ caps the maximum vertical change by at most $M$ times the horizontal step.

rungs.why: By Theorem 5.4.5, any function satisfying $|f(x)-f(y)| \le M|x-y|$ is Lipschitz, hence uniformly continuous.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Capping the steepness everywhere prevents the function from ever tearing or stretching too wildly, ensuring uniform continuity.

title: Darboux’s Theorem (Intermediate Value Property of Derivatives)

rungs.why: Assume without loss of generality $f'(a) < k < f'(b)$ and construct an auxiliary function.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Tilt the function downward by $k$ so that searching for slope $k$ becomes searching for a flat horizontal slope in the helper curve.

rungs.why: $g$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ because $f$ is differentiable (hence continuous). By the Maximum-Minimum Theorem (5.3.4), $g$ attains an absolute minimum at some point $c \in [a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The continuous helper curve must reach an absolute bottom valley somewhere on the closed interval.

rungs.why: Evaluate the derivative of $g$ at the endpoints.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The curve slopes downward moving into the interval from the left, and climbs upward entering from the right.

rungs.why: Since $g'(a) < 0$, $g(x) < g(a)$ for $x > a$ near $a$, so $c \ne a$. Similarly, since $g'(b) > 0$, $g(x) < g(b)$ for $x < b$ near $b$, so $c \ne b$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The valley cannot sit at either border, so it is trapped strictly inside the open interior.

rungs.why: Since $c$ is an interior extremum and $g$ is differentiable at $c$, Fermat's Theorem (6.2.1) applies.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: At the bottom of this internal valley, the tilted slope is zero, meaning the original function hits the target slope $k$ exactly.

rungs.why: First verify $g(b) - g(a) \ne 0$. If $g(b) = g(a)$, Rolle's theorem would imply $g'(\xi) = 0$ for some $\xi \in (a, b)$, contradicting $g' \ne 0$. Now define the auxiliary function $h$ on $[a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Cross-multiply the total displacements of both functions to construct a single helper curve that compares their simultaneous motions.

rungs.why: $h$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$ as a linear combination of $f$ and $g$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The rate of change of the helper function directly tracks the cross-product of the instantaneous velocities.

rungs.why: Evaluate $h$ at the endpoints $a$ and $b$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The helper curve begins and ends at the exact same height, setting up the exact condition needed for Rolle's theorem.

rungs.why: Apply Rolle's Theorem (6.2.3) to $h$ on $[a, b]$, guaranteeing a point $c \in (a, b)$ with $h'(c) = 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Somewhere during the interval, the cross-product balance of instantaneous speeds halts at a momentary equilibrium.

rungs.why: Divide by $[g(b) - g(a)] g'(c)$, valid since both factors are non-zero.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The ratio of total distances covered by the two functions equals the ratio of their instantaneous speeds at some shared moment.

rungs.why: Extend $f$ and $g$ to $[a, b)$ by defining $f(a) = 0$ and $g(a) = 0$. Both are continuous on $[a, x]$ for $x \in (a, b)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Plug the pinhole leak at the starting boundary so both curves start continuously from zero.

rungs.why: Apply Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem (6.3.2) to $f$ and $g$ on $[a, x]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Cauchy's theorem matches the ratio of outputs from the starting point to the ratio of their derivatives at an intermediate point.

rungs.why: Substitute $f(a) = 0$ and $g(a) = 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because both functions started at zero, the ratio of their current values is identical to the ratio of their slopes at some prior instant.

rungs.why: As $x \to a^+$, the squeeze $a < c_x < x$ forces $c_x \to a^+$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: As the window shrinks toward the origin, the intermediate point is squeezed along with it, forcing the function ratio to match the slope ratio.

rungs.why: Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $y \in (a, b)$ such that $|f'(c)/g'(c) - L| < \varepsilon/2$ for all $c \in (a, y)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Anchor a reference point $y$ close to the boundary where the ratio of derivatives has already stabilized near its limit.

rungs.why: Apply Cauchy MVT (6.3.2) on $[x, y]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Express the ratio of changes between the wandering point $x$ and the anchor $y$ as the slope ratio at a point trapped between them.

rungs.why: Multiply by $\frac{g(x) - g(y)}{g(x)}$ and rewrite $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Factor out the dominant exploding terms to show that the anchor values become negligible corrections as $g(x)$ grows huge.

rungs.why: Since $y$ is fixed and $g(x) \to \infty$ as $x \to a^+$, the terms $g(y)/g(x) \to 0$ and $f(y)/g(x) \to 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: As the denominator blows up to infinity, the fixed anchor noise completely washes away, locking the overall ratio onto the derivative ratio.

rungs.why: Fix $x, x_0 \in I$ with $x \ne x_0$. Define the constant $M$ such that $f(x) = P_n(x) + M(x - x_0)^{n+1}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Package the unknown error between the true curve and its polynomial approximation into a single coefficient of the next power.

rungs.why: Define an auxiliary function $F$ on the interval between $x_0$ and $x$ by varying the base point $t$:
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Build an error tracker that slides the expansion center from the base point all the way to the target point.

rungs.why: Observe that $F(x) = 0$, and by choice of $M$, $F(x_0) = 0$. Since $f^{(n+1)}$ exists, $F$ is differentiable.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The sliding error function vanishes at both ends of the interval, perfectly setting up Rolle's theorem.

rungs.why: Differentiate $F(t)$ with respect to $t$. By the product rule, the sum telescopes and successive terms cancel pairwise.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Differentiating causes every intermediate derivative to cancel out in a cascading telescope, leaving only the very top derivative and the error term.

rungs.why: Apply Rolle's Theorem (6.2.3) to $F$ on $[x_0, x]$. There exists $c$ strictly between $x_0$ and $x$ such that $F'(c) = 0$. Since $c \ne x$, $(x - c)^n \ne 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Rolle's theorem locates a point where the balance zeroes out, proving the error coefficient is precisely the next derivative divided by $(n+1)!$.

title: Taylor Remainder Estimates and Maclaurin Expansions

rungs.why: From Taylor’s Theorem (6.4.1), write the Lagrange remainder on $[x_0, x]$.
rungs.m: $$R_n(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n + 1)!}(x - x_0)^{n+1} \quad \text{for some } c \text{ between } x_0, x$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Express the gap between the true function and its polynomial as an exact formula driven by the next derivative at an unknown intermediate point.

rungs.why: Take absolute values and substitute the upper bound $|f^{(n+1)}(c)| \le M$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Replace the unknown intermediate derivative with its worst-case maximum ceiling to get a solid upper bound on the error.

rungs.why: By the Ratio Test for sequences (Theorem 3.2.11), for any fixed real number $A = |x - x_0|$, $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{A^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} = 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Factorial growth in the denominator eventually crushes any fixed power in the numerator down to nothing.

rungs.why: Apply the Squeeze Theorem for sequences (3.2.7) to conclude $\lim_{n\to\infty} R_n(x) = 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the remainder is squeezed to zero, adding more polynomial terms converges to the exact value of the original function.

rungs.why: Suppose $L_1$ and $L_2$ both satisfy the definition of the integral for $f$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $\delta_1, \delta_2 > 0$ for $\varepsilon/2$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Assume two different numbers claim to be the true area, and set an error budget of half-epsilon for each candidate.

rungs.why: Set $\delta = \min\{\delta_1, \delta_2\} > 0$ and choose any tagged partition $\dot{\mathcal{P}}$ with $\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}\| < \delta$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Slice the interval finely enough that a single Riemann sum must satisfy both candidate limits simultaneously.

rungs.why: Apply the Triangle Inequality to $|L_1 - L_2|$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Route the gap between the two rival limits through that one shared Riemann sum using the triangle inequality.

rungs.why: Sum the tolerances: $\varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Combining the two half-tolerances proves the distance between the two candidates is strictly less than epsilon.

rungs.why: Since $\varepsilon > 0$ is arbitrary, by Theorem 2.1.9, $|L_1 - L_2| = 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Two fixed constants separated by less than any positive margin must be the exact same number, guaranteeing the integral is unique.

rungs.why: Suppose for contradiction that $f \in \mathcal{R}[0, 1]$ with integral $L$. Set $\varepsilon_0 = 1/2$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Assume for contradiction that an overall area exists, so every fine enough approximation must land within a half-unit of that area.

rungs.why: Let $\mathcal{P}$ be any partition of $[0, 1]$ with $\|\mathcal{P}\| < \delta$. By density of $\mathbb{Q}$ (2.4.8), choose rational tags $t_i \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [x_{i-1}, x_i]$ for all $i$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: By choosing only rational sample points in every slice where the function equals 1, the total Riemann sum is forced to be 1.

rungs.why: By density of irrationals (2.4.9), choose irrational tags $s_i \notin \mathbb{Q} \cap [x_{i-1}, x_i]$ for all $i$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: On that very same partition, choosing only irrational sample points where the function equals 0 forces the Riemann sum to be 0.

rungs.why: Both tagged partitions have norm $< \delta$, so both sums must be within $1/2$ of $L$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The putative limit would have to sit simultaneously within a half-unit radius of both 1 and 0.

rungs.why: Apply the Triangle Inequality: $1 = |1 - 0| \le |1 - L| + |L - 0| < 1/2 + 1/2 = 1$, yielding $1 < 1$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The distance between 0 and 1 is 1, which cannot be strictly less than 1, proving the function is too violently discontinuous to be integrable.

title: Linearity and Monotonicity of the Riemann Integral

rungs.why: For any tagged partition $\dot{\mathcal{P}}$, write the Riemann sum of $\alpha f + \beta g$.
rungs.m: $$S(\alpha f + \beta g; \dot{\mathcal{P}}) = \sum_{i=1}^n [\alpha f(t_i) + \beta g(t_i)](x_i - x_{i-1}) = \alpha S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}) + \beta S(g; \dot{\mathcal{P}})$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Finite sums naturally distribute over addition and scalar multiples, splitting the composite Riemann sum into individual sums.

rungs.why: Let $L_1 = \int_a^b f$ and $L_2 = \int_a^b g$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $\delta > 0$ such that for $\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}\| < \delta$, $|S(f) - L_1| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2(|\alpha| + 1)}$ and $|S(g) - L_2| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2(|\beta| + 1)}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Choose a fine partition that controls the individual errors for both integrals, scaled down by their respective coefficients.

rungs.why: Combine the terms using the Triangle Inequality.
rungs.m: $$|S(\alpha f + \beta g) - (\alpha L_1 + \beta L_2)| \le |\alpha| |S(f) - L_1| + |\beta| |S(g) - L_2| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The scaled error bounds add up to less than epsilon, proving that the integral of the combination is the combination of the integrals.

rungs.why: For monotonicity: if $f \le g$, every term $f(t_i)(x_i - x_{i-1}) \le g(t_i)(x_i - x_{i-1})$, so $S(f) \le S(g)$. Taking limits preserves inequalities.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: A taller curve produces taller approximating rectangles in every slice, so its total accumulated area can never be smaller.

rungs.why: Suppose $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$ with integral $L$. Choose $\delta > 0$ such that for every tagged partition $\dot{\mathcal{P}}$ with $\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}\| < \delta$, $|S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}) - L| < 1$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If an integral exists, every sufficiently fine Riemann sum is trapped within a fixed ceiling.

rungs.why: Let $\mathcal{P} = \{x_0, \ldots, x_n\}$ be an untagged partition with $\|\mathcal{P}\| < \delta$. If $f$ were bounded on every subinterval $I_i = [x_{i-1}, x_i]$, $f$ would be bounded on $[a, b]$. Thus $f$ is unbounded on at least one subinterval $I_k$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If the function were unbounded overall, the infinite blow-up must be housed inside at least one specific subinterval.

rungs.why: Fix arbitrary tags $t_i$ for all other subintervals $i \ne k$. Let $S^* = \sum_{i \ne k} f(t_i)(x_i - x_{i-1})$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Freeze the contributions of all innocent subintervals into a constant base, leaving only the rogue subinterval free to vary.

rungs.why: Since $f$ is unbounded on $I_k$, choose $t_k \in I_k$ such that $|f(t_k)| > \frac{|L| + 1 + |S^*|}{x_k - x_{k-1}}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Pick a single tag inside the rogue subinterval where the function value spikes high enough to overpower the sum of all other slices combined.

rungs.why: By the reverse triangle inequality, $|S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}})| \ge |f(t_k)|(x_k - x_{k-1}) - |S^*| > |L| + 1$, contradicting the bound from step 1.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: This single towering rectangle blows the entire Riemann sum past the permissible ceiling, proving integrable functions must be bounded.

title: The Cauchy Criterion for Riemann Integrability

rungs.why: (=>) Assume $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$ with integral $L$. Choose $\delta > 0$ for $\varepsilon/2$. For $\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}\|, \|\dot{\mathcal{Q}}\| < \delta$, both $|S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}) - L| < \varepsilon/2$ and $|S(f; \dot{\mathcal{Q}}) - L| < \varepsilon/2$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If all fine approximations approach a common target, any two of them must stay within epsilon of each other.

rungs.why: (<=) Assume the Cauchy condition. For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, choose $\delta_n > 0$ corresponding to $\varepsilon = 1/n$, with $\delta_{n+1} \le \delta_n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Assume any two fine Riemann sums stay arbitrarily close, and create an increasingly strict series of mesh limits.

rungs.why: Choose a sequence of tagged partitions $\dot{\mathcal{P}}_n$ with $\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}_n\| < \delta_n$. For $m > n$, both norms are $< \delta_n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Construct a sequence of Riemann sums that cluster progressively tighter together.

rungs.why: Thus $(S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}_n))$ is a Cauchy sequence of real numbers. By completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ (3.5.5), it converges to some limit $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the real numbers have no holes, any sequence of numbers clustering together is guaranteed to converge to an actual limit.

rungs.why: For any tagged partition $\dot{\mathcal{Q}}$ with $\|\dot{\mathcal{Q}}\| < \delta_K$ (where $1/K < \varepsilon/2$), $|S(f; \dot{\mathcal{Q}}) - L| \le |S(f; \dot{\mathcal{Q}}) - S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}_K)| + |S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}_K) - L| < \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Any other fine partition is trapped near the sequence limit, proving the function converges unconditionally to this integral value.

title: The Squeeze Theorem for Riemann Integrability

rungs.why: (=>) If $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$, choose $\alpha_\varepsilon = \omega_\varepsilon = f$. Then $\int_a^b (\omega_\varepsilon - \alpha_\varepsilon) = 0 < \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: An already integrable function brackets itself perfectly with zero gap between the upper and lower bounds.

rungs.why: (<=) Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $\alpha_\varepsilon, \omega_\varepsilon \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$, choose $\delta > 0$ such that for $\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}\| < \delta$, $|S(\alpha_\varepsilon; \dot{\mathcal{P}}) - \int \alpha_\varepsilon| < \varepsilon$ and $|S(\omega_\varepsilon; \dot{\mathcal{P}}) - \int \omega_\varepsilon| < \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Trap the unknown function's Riemann sum between the reliable Riemann sums of its lower and upper guardrail functions.

rungs.why: For any two tagged partitions $\dot{\mathcal{P}}, \dot{\mathcal{Q}}$ with norm $< \delta$, both $S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}})$ and $S(f; \dot{\mathcal{Q}})$ lie in $(\int \alpha_\varepsilon - \varepsilon, \int \omega_\varepsilon + \varepsilon)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Any two arbitrary approximations of the function are squeezed into the narrow corridor between the two guardrails.

rungs.why: Substitute the hypothesis $\int_a^b (\omega_\varepsilon - \alpha_\varepsilon) < \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the area gap between the guardrails is tiny, the gap between any two Riemann sums is throttled down to three epsilon.

rungs.why: By the Cauchy Criterion (7.2.1), $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Squeezing the sums into an arbitrarily tight band satisfies the Cauchy criterion, proving the function is fully integrable.

rungs.why: Let $J$ be any subinterval of $[a, b]$ with endpoints $c < d$. Let $\varphi_J$ be the indicator function: $\varphi_J(x) = 1$ on $J$ and $0$ elsewhere.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Start with a single rectangular block that is 1 over an interval and 0 everywhere else.

rungs.why: For any tagged partition $\dot{\mathcal{P}}$ with mesh $\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}\| < \delta$, Riemann sums $S(\varphi_J; \dot{\mathcal{P}})$ differ from $d - c$ by at most $2\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}\| < 2\delta$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Any error in capturing the block only happens at its two boundary cuts, which shrink to zero as the partition gets finer.

rungs.why: Every step function $\varphi$ is a finite linear combination of elementary step functions: $\varphi = \sum_{j=1}^m k_j \varphi_{J_j}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Any staircase function is just a finite set of these simple rectangular blocks stacked or placed side-by-side.

rungs.why: Apply Linearity of the Integral (Theorem 7.1.5) to the finite sum.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Integrating the staircase is simply adding up the basic width-times-height areas of each flat step.

rungs.why: By Theorem 5.4.3, $f$ is uniformly continuous on $[a, b]$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $\delta > 0$ such that $|u - v| < \delta \implies |f(u) - f(v)| < \frac{\varepsilon}{b - a}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: On a closed interval, continuity is uniform, meaning points close together cannot fluctuate in height by more than a tiny budget.

rungs.why: Let $\mathcal{P} = \{x_0, \ldots, x_n\}$ be a partition with mesh $\|\mathcal{P}\| < \delta$. By the Maximum-Minimum Theorem (5.3.4), $f$ attains a min $f(u_i)$ and max $f(v_i)$ on each $I_i$.
rungs.m: $$m_i = f(u_i), \quad M_i = f(v_i) \quad \text{with } u_i, v_i \in I_i$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Inside each narrow slice, the curve reaches an absolute top ceiling and an absolute bottom floor.

rungs.why: Since $|u_i - v_i| \le \|\mathcal{P}\| < \delta$, the oscillation satisfies $M_i - m_i < \frac{\varepsilon}{b - a}$ for all $i$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the slice is narrower than delta, the vertical gap between the ceiling and floor is smaller than the target margin.

rungs.why: Define step functions $\alpha_\varepsilon(x) = m_i$ and $\omega_\varepsilon(x) = M_i$ on each $(x_{i-1}, x_i)$. Then $\alpha_\varepsilon \le f \le \omega_\varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Sandwiched between lower and upper staircase functions, the total area gap across all slices collapses to less than epsilon.

rungs.why: By the Squeeze Theorem (7.2.3), $f$ is Riemann integrable.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the staircase trap closes as tight as desired, every continuous function is proven to be Riemann integrable.

rungs.why: Assume $f$ is increasing on $[a, b]$. Divide $[a, b]$ into $n$ equal subintervals of length $h = (b - a)/n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Slice the domain evenly into $n$ identical strips of equal width.

rungs.why: On $I_i = [x_{i-1}, x_i]$, the infimum is $f(x_{i-1})$ and supremum is $f(x_i)$. Define step functions $\alpha_n(x) = f(x_{i-1})$ and $\omega_n(x) = f(x_i)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: For an increasing function, the left edge is always the bottom floor and the right edge is always the top ceiling.

rungs.why: Integrate $\omega_n - \alpha_n$: factor out the common width $(b - a)/n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The total uncertainty area is the uniform strip width multiplied by the sum of all the vertical step heights.

rungs.why: The sum telescopes completely: all intermediate terms cancel!
rungs.meaning: What this really means: All intermediate elevations cancel out completely, collapsing the sum of step heights into simply the total climb from start to finish.

rungs.why: Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $n > \frac{(b - a)(f(b) - f(a))}{\varepsilon}$. Then $\int_a^b (\omega_n - \alpha_n) < \varepsilon$, and the Squeeze Theorem (7.2.3) applies.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Making $n$ large shrinks the uncertainty to zero, proving monotone functions are always integrable regardless of how many jumps they have.

title: Additivity of the Integral over Subintervals

rungs.why: Let $L_1 = \int_a^c f$ and $L_2 = \int_c^b f$. Let $M$ be a bound for $|f|$ on $[a, b]$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $\delta > 0$ with $\delta < \frac{\varepsilon}{6M}$ such that subinterval sums are within $\varepsilon/3$ of $L_1, L_2$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Budget a one-third epsilon tolerance for the left region, the right region, and any straddling boundary slice.

rungs.why: Let $\dot{\mathcal{P}}$ be a tagged partition of $[a, b]$ with $\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}\| < \delta$. If $c$ is a partition point, $\dot{\mathcal{P}}$ splits into $\dot{\mathcal{P}}_1$ and $\dot{\mathcal{P}}_2$, and $S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}) = S(f_1; \dot{\mathcal{P}}_1) + S(f_2; \dot{\mathcal{P}}_2)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If the split point $c$ lands cleanly on a partition line, the two sub-sums add up to the total sum effortlessly.

rungs.why: If $c$ is inside a subinterval $(x_{k-1}, x_k)$, insert $c$ with tag $c$ into both $[x_{k-1}, c]$ and $[c, x_k]$ to form partitions $\dot{\mathcal{Q}}_1, \dot{\mathcal{Q}}_2$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If $c$ falls inside a slice, snapping it to the boundary creates an error that is strictly bounded by the slice width times the function bound.

rungs.why: Combine the triangle inequality terms: $\varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 = \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Adding the three fractional errors keeps the total within epsilon, proving the total area is the exact sum of the two sub-areas.

title: Integrability of Absolute Value and Triangle Inequality for Integrals

rungs.why: By the reverse triangle inequality (2.2.1), for any $u, v \in [a, b]$, $||f(u)| - |f(v)|| \le |f(u) - f(v)|$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Folding negative values upward with absolute values can only pull points closer together, never push them further apart.

rungs.why: Taking supremum over subinterval $I_i$, the oscillation of $|f|$ is bounded by the oscillation of $f$:
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The height difference between the peak and valley of $|f|$ in any slice is at most that of the original function $f$.

rungs.why: Multiply by subinterval widths: $U(|f|, \mathcal{P}) - L(|f|, \mathcal{P}) \le U(f, \mathcal{P}) - L(f, \mathcal{P}) < \varepsilon$. By the Squeeze Theorem (7.2.3), $|f| \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because $|f|$ fluctuates less than $f$ on every slice, its total uncertainty gap is even smaller, guaranteeing that $|f|$ is integrable.

rungs.why: Since $-|f(x)| \le f(x) \le |f(x)|$, apply Monotonicity of Integrals (Theorem 7.1.5).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Bounding the original curve between its inverted absolute value and its positive absolute value carries directly over to their integrals.

rungs.why: Translate this double inequality into absolute value notation.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Net signed area (where peaks and valleys cancel out) can never exceed total gross area (where every region counts as positive).

title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (First Form: Evaluation of Integrals)

rungs.why: Assume $E = \emptyset$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$, choose $\delta > 0$ such that $\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}\| < \delta \implies |S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}) - \int_a^b f| < \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because $f$ is integrable, every fine enough Riemann sum is trapped arbitrarily close to the true integral.

rungs.why: Let $\mathcal{P} = \{x_0, \ldots, x_n\}$ have mesh $< \delta$. By Lagrange MVT (6.2.4), on each $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$, there exists $u_i \in (x_{i-1}, x_i)$ with $F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) = F'(u_i)(x_i - x_{i-1})$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The Mean Value Theorem finds a magic tag in every slice where the slice's rectangle exactly equals the antiderivative change.

rungs.why: Sum over all subintervals: the left side telescopes to $F(b) - F(a)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Adding up these increments causes all intermediate partition values to cancel out, leaving just the net change $F(b) - F(a)$.

rungs.why: Notice that $\sum f(u_i)(x_i - x_{i-1})$ is precisely the Riemann sum $S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}_u)$ with tags $u_i$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The net change of the antiderivative is identical to an actual, valid Riemann sum formed with those magic tags.

rungs.why: Since $\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}_u\| < \delta$, substitute into the integrability bound: $|F(b) - F(a) - \int_a^b f| < \varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon > 0$ is arbitrary, equality holds.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because this equality holds within every tolerance epsilon, the total accumulated area must be exactly $F(b) - F(a)$.

title: First Mean Value Theorem for Integrals

rungs.why: By the Maximum-Minimum Theorem (5.3.4), $f$ attains an absolute minimum $m$ and maximum $M$ on $[a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: A continuous function on a closed interval stays bounded between its absolute lowest floor and highest ceiling.

rungs.why: Apply Monotonicity of Integrals (Theorem 7.1.5).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The true area under the curve is trapped between the minimum bounding box and the maximum bounding box.

rungs.why: Divide by $(b - a) > 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The average height of the curve lies comfortably between its lowest and highest values.

rungs.why: The number $k = \frac{1}{b - a} \int_a^b f$ lies in $[m, M]$. By Bolzano’s Intermediate Value Theorem (5.3.7), $f$ attains $k$ at some $c \in [a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: A continuous curve cannot skip any intermediate heights, so it must hit its exact average height at some point.

title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Second Form: Differentiation of an Integral)

rungs.why: Write the difference quotient for $F$ at $c$ for $h \ne 0$. By additivity (7.2.9), $F(c+h) - F(c) = \int_c^{c+h} f(t)\,dt$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The average rate of accumulation over a step of width $h$ is simply the average height of the function across that step.

rungs.why: Since $\frac{1}{h}\int_c^{c+h} f(c)\,dt = f(c) \cdot \frac{h}{h} = f(c)$, subtract $f(c)$ inside the integral.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Comparing the average step height to the instantaneous height $f(c)$ amounts to averaging the height differences across the window.

rungs.why: Since $f$ is continuous at $c$, given $\varepsilon > 0$, $\exists \delta > 0$ such that $|t - c| < \delta \implies |f(t) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the function is continuous at $c$, shrinking the window traps all values within epsilon of $f(c)$.

rungs.why: For $0 < |h| < \delta$, apply the integral triangle inequality (7.2.10).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The average fluctuation across the tiny window shrinks to zero, proving the derivative of the area accumulation is the height itself.

rungs.why: Define $F(u) = \int_{\varphi(\alpha)}^u f(x)\,dx$ for $u \in I$. Since $f$ is continuous, by FTC Form 2 (7.3.5), $F'(u) = f(u)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Set up the antiderivative of $f$ using an accumulation function, whose derivative is $f$ by the Fundamental Theorem.

rungs.why: Define the composite function $H(t) = F(\varphi(t))$ on $J = [\alpha, \beta]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Re-parametrize the area accumulation according to the new time or variable scale $t$.

rungs.why: By the Chain Rule (6.1.5), $H$ is differentiable on $J$ with $H'(t) = F'(\varphi(t))\varphi'(t) = f(\varphi(t))\varphi'(t)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The chain rule shows the new rate of accumulation is the original curve height multiplied by the speed of the coordinate stretching.

rungs.why: Since $H'$ is continuous, apply FTC Form 1 (7.3.1) to $H$ on $[\alpha, \beta]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Integrating this transformed rate over the new interval gives the net change in $H$.

rungs.why: Evaluate $H(\beta) - H(\alpha) = F(\varphi(\beta)) - F(\varphi(\alpha)) = \int_{\varphi(\alpha)}^{\varphi(\beta)} f(u)\,du - 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Evaluating the net change connects the transformed integral directly to the original area between transformed limits.

rungs.why: Let $D_\alpha = \{x \in [a, b] : \omega_f(x) \ge \alpha\}$ be the points where oscillation of $f$ is at least $\alpha > 0$. $D = \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty D_{1/k}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Classify all discontinuity jump points according to the minimum size of their jump.

rungs.why: If $\mu(D) = 0$, then each $D_\alpha$ has measure zero and is compact, so it can be covered by finitely many open intervals of total length $< \varepsilon/(4M)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the set of jumps is negligible, all large jumps can be fenced off inside tiny enclosures of negligible total width.

rungs.why: Outside this cover, $f$ has oscillation $< \varepsilon/(2(b - a))$ on the compact remainder, which can be covered by subintervals where $M_i - m_i < \varepsilon/(2(b - a))$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: On the vast peaceful remainder where the function behaves, the total approximation gap stays under half-epsilon.

rungs.why: On the bad subintervals covering $D_\alpha$, $M_i - m_i \le 2M$, so their sum is bounded by $2M \sum |J_k| < 2M \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{4M} = \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Even though the function jumps wild inside the fenced enclosures, their total width is so tiny that their area error stays under half-epsilon.

rungs.why: Total gap $U(f, \mathcal{P}) - L(f, \mathcal{P}) < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon$. By Darboux Criterion (7.4.8), $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Combining the peaceful regions and tiny fenced enclosures keeps the total area error below epsilon, proving Riemann integrability.

rungs.why: By the Product Rule (6.1.3), $(fg)'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x)$ for all $x \in [a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Recall that the derivative of a product splits into two terms, each differentiating one factor at a time.

rungs.why: Since $f, g, f', g'$ are continuous, the products $f'g$ and $fg'$ are Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Smoothness ensures that all product terms are continuous and can be integrated without issue.

rungs.why: Integrate both sides over $[a, b]$ using Linearity of Integrals (7.1.5).
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Integrating the entire equation preserves the sum on both sides.

rungs.why: Apply FTC Form 1 (7.3.1) to the left side: $\int_a^b (fg)' = f(b)g(b) - f(a)g(a)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The Fundamental Theorem evaluates the integral of the total derivative directly from its boundary values.

rungs.why: Rearrange to isolate $\int_a^b f(x)g'(x)\,dx$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Shifting one term to the other side lets you trade an intractable integral for a boundary term minus a friendlier integral.

rungs.why: By FTC Form 2 (7.3.5), write $f(x) - f(x_0) = \int_{x_0}^x f'(t)\,dt$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Start with the baseline truth that a function's current value is its starting value plus the integral of its velocity.

rungs.why: Apply Integration by Parts (7.3.17) with $u = f'(t)$ and $v = -(x - t)$. Note $v' = 1$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Integrating by parts with a clever linear factor extracts the first tangent term and produces a second-order remainder.

rungs.why: This proves the formula for $n = 1$: $f(x) = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0) + \int_{x_0}^x (x - t)f''(t)\,dt$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The function is now cleanly split into its degree-one tangent line plus an exact weighted integral error.

rungs.why: Integrate by parts again with $u = f''(t)$ and $v = -\frac{(x - t)^2}{2}$. The boundary term produces $\frac{f''(x_0)}{2!}(x - x_0)^2$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Repeating integration by parts pulls out the quadratic curvature term and pushes the remainder to the third derivative.

rungs.why: By induction on $n$, continuing $n$ times produces the full polynomial $P_n(x)$ and integral remainder.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Continuing the process $n$ times generates the complete Taylor polynomial with an exact integral formula for the remaining error.

rungs.why: (=>) Let $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$ with integral $I$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $\delta > 0$ such that for any tagged partition with mesh $< \delta$, $|S(f) - I| < \varepsilon/4$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Assume the Riemann integral exists, trapping every fine tagged sum within a tight quarter-epsilon neighborhood of the true area.

rungs.why: For any fixed partition $\mathcal{P}$ of mesh $< \delta$, choose tags $t_i$ such that $f(t_i) > M_i - \frac{\varepsilon}{4(b-a)}$ and $s_i$ such that $f(s_i) < m_i + \frac{\varepsilon}{4(b-a)}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Pick sample tags so high that the Riemann sum pushes close to the Upper Darboux sum, and others so low they push close to the Lower Darboux sum.

rungs.why: Subtract the inequalities: $U(f, \mathcal{P}) - L(f, \mathcal{P}) < S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}_t) - S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}_s) + \varepsilon/2 < \varepsilon/4 + \varepsilon/4 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because both tagged sums are trapped near the same integral, the gap between the upper and lower Darboux bounds is forced below epsilon.

rungs.why: (<=) Conversely, if $U(f, \mathcal{P}_\varepsilon) - L(f, \mathcal{P}_\varepsilon) < \varepsilon$, then since $\underline{\int} f \ge L(f, \mathcal{P})$ and $\overline{\int} f \le U(f, \mathcal{P})$, $0 \le \overline{\int} f - \underline{\int} f < \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Squeezing the upper and lower Darboux sums together forces the upper and lower integrals to coincide, matching the Riemann integral.

rungs.why: (=>) Assume $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to $f$ on $A$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $K(\varepsilon)$ such that for all $n \ge K(\varepsilon)$ and all $x \in A$, $|f_n(x) - f(x)| \le \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Uniform convergence guarantees that past a certain stage, every single point on the graph simultaneously lies within epsilon of the target curve.

rungs.why: By definition of the supremum as least upper bound, taking supremum over $x \in A$ preserves the inequality.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If every individual point is within epsilon, then even the single worst-case point on the entire domain cannot exceed epsilon.

rungs.why: Since $\varepsilon > 0$ is arbitrary, $\lim_{n\to\infty} \|f_n - f\|_A = 0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The maximum peak error across the entire domain shrinks to zero like a regular sequence of real numbers.

rungs.why: (<=) Conversely, assume $\lim_{n\to\infty} \|f_n - f\|_A = 0$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $H(\varepsilon)$ such that $\|f_n - f\|_A < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge H(\varepsilon)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Assume the worst-case peak error across the domain shrinks to zero.

rungs.why: For any $x \in A$, $|f_n(x) - f(x)| \le \|f_n - f\|_A < \varepsilon$, which proves uniform convergence.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Since every point is bounded by the peak error, holding the peak below epsilon traps all points simultaneously, proving uniform convergence.

rungs.why: Write the definition of uniform convergence: $\forall \varepsilon > 0, \, \exists K \in \mathbb{N}, \, \forall n \ge K, \, \forall x \in A : |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$.
rungs.m: $$\forall \varepsilon > 0 \, \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \, \forall n \ge K \, \forall x \in A : |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: For convergence to be uniform, one single cutoff index must force every single point on the domain within epsilon of the limit.

rungs.why: Negate this statement by flipping quantifiers.
rungs.m: $$\exists \varepsilon_0 > 0 \, \forall K \in \mathbb{N} \, \exists n \ge K, \, \exists x \in A : |f_n(x) - f(x)| \ge \varepsilon_0$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Non-uniformity means there is a fixed error barrier such that no matter how far down the sequence you look, some runaway point still fails.

rungs.why: For $K = 1$, choose $n_1 \ge 1$ and $x_1 \in A$ such that $|f_{n_1}(x_1) - f(x_1)| \ge \varepsilon_0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Pick the very first function index and rogue location where the error fails the barrier.

rungs.why: Inductively, for $K_m = n_{m-1} + 1$, choose $n_m > n_{m-1}$ and $x_m \in A$ with $|f_{n_m}(x_m) - f(x_m)| \ge \varepsilon_0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: March endlessly down the sequence, picking a moving runaway point for each step to construct a concrete trail of failure.

rungs.why: (=>) If $f_n \to f$ uniformly on $A$, choose $K(\varepsilon/2)$ such that $n \ge K \implies |f_n(x) - f(x)| \le \varepsilon/2$ for all $x$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: If the sequence uniformly clusters around a limit curve, any two late function graphs must stay within epsilon of each other.

rungs.why: Taking supremum over $x \in A$ gives $\|f_m - f_n\|_A \le \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The maximum separation between any two late curves across the whole domain is bounded by epsilon.

rungs.why: (<=) Assume the Cauchy condition. For each fixed $x \in A$, $(f_n(x))$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb{R}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: At each individual point, the output numbers form a standard Cauchy sequence of real numbers.

rungs.why: By completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ (Theorem 3.5.5), $(f_n(x))$ converges in $\mathbb{R}$. Define $f(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(x)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Completeness of the real numbers guarantees that each point's sequence of values converges to an unambiguous destination.

rungs.why: Keep $m \ge H(\varepsilon)$ fixed and send $n \to \infty$ in $|f_m(x) - f_n(x)| \le \varepsilon$. By Theorem 3.2.6, limits preserve weak inequalities.
rungs.m: $$|f_m(x) - f(x)| = \lim_{n\to\infty} |f_m(x) - f_n(x)| \le \varepsilon \quad \forall x \in A, \, m \ge H(\varepsilon)$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Passing to the limit preserves the uniform tolerance, proving that the sequence converges uniformly to this constructed limit function.

title: The Uniform Limit Theorem (Preservation of Continuity)

rungs.why: Split the total change using the triangle inequality with an intermediate $f_n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Route the change in the limit function through an intermediate continuous member of the sequence using three short hops.

rungs.why: Choose $N$ such that for all $n \ge N$ and all $t \in A$, $|f_n(t) - f(t)| < \varepsilon/3$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Use uniform convergence to pick a curve so close to the limit that jumping between them at both ends costs under a third of epsilon.

rungs.why: Since $f_N$ is continuous at $c$, choose $\delta > 0$ such that $|x - c| < \delta \implies |f_N(x) - f_N(c)| < \varepsilon/3$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because that intermediate curve is continuous, taking a sufficiently small step along it costs under a third of epsilon.

rungs.why: Combine all three $\varepsilon/3$ bounds.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Adding the three hops keeps the total vertical change under epsilon, proving that the limit function is strictly continuous.

rungs.why: For any $x \in J$, apply MVT (6.2.4) to $f_m - f_n$ on the interval between $x_0$ and $x$.
rungs.m: $$f_m(x) - f_n(x) = f_m(x_0) - f_n(x_0) + (x - x_0)[f_m'(y) - f_n'(y)] \quad \text{for some } y$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The Mean Value Theorem expresses the difference between two functions as their baseline difference plus their slope difference.

rungs.why: Since $(f_n(x_0))$ converges and $(f_n')$ is uniformly Cauchy, $(f_n)$ is uniformly Cauchy on $J$, so $f_n \to f$ uniformly on $J$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Because the slopes cluster uniformly and one point converges, the functions themselves are forced to converge uniformly.

rungs.why: For fixed $c \in J$ and $x \ne c$, apply MVT to $(f_m - f_n)$ on $[c, x]$: $\frac{f_m(x)-f_m(c)}{x-c} - \frac{f_n(x)-f_n(c)}{x-c} = f_m'(z) - f_n'(z)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Secant slopes of the functions cluster uniformly because the derivatives controlling them cluster uniformly.

rungs.why: Take $m \to \infty$: $|\frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} - \frac{f_n(x) - f_n(c)}{x - c}| \le \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Sending $m$ to infinity shows the secant slope of the limit function stays within epsilon of the secant slope of $f_n$.

rungs.why: Combine with $|f_n'(c) - g(c)| < \varepsilon$ and differentiability of $f_n$ at $c$ to conclude $|\frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} - g(c)| < 3\varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The limit function's derivative exists and matches the uniform limit of the derivatives: $(lim f_n)' = lim (f_n')$.

rungs.why: Given $\varepsilon > 0$, by Cauchy Criterion (8.1.10), $\exists H(\varepsilon)$ such that for $m > n \ge H$, $-\varepsilon \le f_m(x) - f_n(x) \le \varepsilon$ for all $x \in [a, b]$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: When functions stay uniformly within epsilon of each other, the difference between their total areas cannot exceed epsilon times the interval length.

rungs.why: Thus $(\int_a^b f_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb{R}$, hence converges to some limit $A = \lim_{n\to\infty} \int_a^b f_n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The sequence of real area numbers forms a Cauchy sequence, so completeness guarantees it converges to a definite limit $A$.

rungs.why: Since $f_n \to f$ uniformly, choose $K$ such that for $m \ge K$, $|f_m(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all $x \in [a, b]$. For any tagged partition $\dot{\mathcal{P}}$, $|S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}) - S(f_m; \dot{\mathcal{P}})| \le \varepsilon(b - a)$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Any Riemann sum of the limit function is tightly bound to the Riemann sum of a late sequence member.

rungs.why: Pick $m$ so large that $|\int_a^b f_m - A| < \varepsilon$. Since $f_m$ is integrable, choose $\delta > 0$ such that $\|\dot{\mathcal{P}}\| < \delta \implies |S(f_m; \dot{\mathcal{P}}) - \int_a^b f_m| < \varepsilon$.
rungs.m: $$|S(f; \dot{\mathcal{P}}) - A| \le |S(f) - S(f_m)| + |S(f_m) - \int f_m| + |\int f_m - A| < \varepsilon(b - a) + 2\varepsilon$$
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Route the Riemann sum of $f$ to the target area $A$ through $f_m$, keeping the total discrepancy arbitrarily small.

rungs.why: Since $\varepsilon > 0$ is arbitrary, $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$ and $\int_a^b f = A = \lim_{n\to\infty} \int_a^b f_n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The limit function is fully integrable, and the integral of the limit equals the limit of the integrals.

title: Bounded Convergence Theorem for Riemann Integrals

rungs.why: Let $g_n = |f_n - f|$. Then $g_n(x) \to 0$ pointwise on $[a, b]$, and $|g_n(x)| \le 2M$ for all $x, n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Look at the absolute gap function, which shrinks to zero at every point while staying capped beneath a universal ceiling $2M$.

rungs.why: Given $\varepsilon > 0$, by Arzelà's theorem, the set of points where $g_n(x) \ge \frac{\varepsilon}{2(b-a)}$ can be enclosed in subintervals of total length $< \frac{\varepsilon}{4M}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The troublesome spots where the gap remains noticeable can be trapped in a tiny total footprint whose area contribution is at most half-epsilon.

rungs.why: On the remaining good set, $g_n(x) < \frac{\varepsilon}{2(b-a)}$, so its integral is bounded by $\frac{\varepsilon}{2(b-a)}(b - a) = \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Across the rest of the domain, the gap is tiny everywhere, so its area contribution is also at most half-epsilon.

rungs.why: Combine both parts: $\int_a^b |f_n - f| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Combining the well-behaved region and the tiny troubled footprint keeps the total area error below epsilon, validating limit-integral swap under bounded pointwise convergence.

title: Dini’s Theorem on Monotone Sequences of Functions

rungs.why: Assume without loss of generality that $(f_n)$ is decreasing. Let $g_n = f_n - f$. Then each $g_n$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, $g_{n+1}(x) \le g_n(x)$, and $g_n(x) \to 0$ for each $x$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Subtract the continuous limit to get a sequence of continuous non-negative functions that march downward to zero at every point.

rungs.why: Suppose for contradiction that $g_n$ does not converge uniformly to $0$. Then $\exists \varepsilon_0 > 0$ such that $\|g_n\|_{[a, b]} \ge \varepsilon_0$ for all $n$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Assume for contradiction that uniform convergence fails, meaning every curve in the sequence maintains a peak at or above a fixed height.

rungs.why: Since $g_n$ is continuous on compact $[a, b]$, by Maximum-Minimum Theorem (5.3.4), $g_n$ attains its maximum at some $x_n \in [a, b]$: $g_n(x_n) \ge \varepsilon_0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: On a compact interval, each continuous curve actually attains its peak at a specific point $x_n$.

rungs.why: By Bolzano-Weierstrass (3.4.8), $(x_n)$ has a subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ converging to some $x^* \in [a, b]$. For any fixed $m$, when $n_k \ge m$, monotonicity gives $g_m(x_{n_k}) \ge g_{n_k}(x_{n_k}) \ge \varepsilon_0$.
rungs.meaning: What this really means: The sequence of peak locations clusters around a limit point $x^*$, and monotonicity ensures an earlier function was at least as tall there.

rungs.why: Take $k \to \infty$: by continuity of $g_m$, $g_m(x^*) = \lim_{k\to\infty} g_m(x_{n_k}) \ge \varepsilon_0$. But this holds for ALL $m$, contradicting $g_m(x^*) \to 0$!
rungs.meaning: What this really means: Passing to the limit forces that single cluster point to stay stubbornly above the threshold for all functions, contradicting pointwise convergence to zero.
